garage.name: Whip Equipped Garage
garage.category: Story hub, workshop, and tire bay
garage.tagline: Every vehicle has a before and after.
garage.description: McCluster, Majid, and Gunny anchor an enterable garage where district stories meet the existing Whip Equipped chapters.
garage.backstory: The garage is a new playable setting for the existing fictional story, presented as a visit before the finale. Its workshop and tire bay give the cast a practical reason to gather. The chapter hub opens the separately maintained screenplay and road-years material rather than replacing long scenes with short NPC exchanges.
ads: WHIP EQUIPPED. Pull into the story.
The next job starts with the whole situation.

interior.style: Familiar working garage with a tire bay and chapter desk
interior.description: A workshop bench, tire stack, and three gathering spots keep the garage readable. A chapter desk leads into the existing long-form story; it is not a replacement for its before/song/after structure.

story.chapterContract: Each chapter preserves before-dialogue 2× song length, the complete uninterrupted song, and after-dialogue 2× song length. Adjacent scenes are not counted twice; the music video has its own expressive staging.
story.mrLockChanger: Keep both perspectives: McCluster’s legitimate service work and the cousin’s criminal misuse of the tablet received from him, with police anxiety, imitation, and humor. This is not a technical theft tutorial.
story.alana: Alana is the same loved character from Test Drive, personifies Atlanta becoming a trap, and dies in Tears Won’t Fall. She is not a permanent post-ending city resident; later appearances require clearly framed memory or subjective imagery.
story.roadYearEvidence: The three initial camper/G20/Econoline entries are owner recollections, tentatively 2024. Photos, dates, transaction amounts, and costs need later reconciliation; the two van sales remain different deals.

garageCrew.name: McCluster
garageCrew.role: Garage owner and Whip Equipped story contact
garageCrew.backstory: McCluster is the existing fictional Whip Equipped protagonist. The garage puts his practical work, relationships, and business ambitions in the same room rather than turning him into a detached mission dispenser. Current story canon preserves his legitimate service work alongside knowingly accepted criminal capital and the choices that follow. The city does not rewrite that tension as either complete innocence or a claim about the owner’s real company. His dialogue here belongs to a chapter-selection visit before the finale. The road-years material provides separate remembered legitimate flips whose approximate dates and costs remain qualified in their source documents. Ages, historical origin, likeness, and any new personal biography remain unassigned by this city expansion.
garageCrew.personality: Resourceful, restless, humorous; wants ownership of his work and must answer for his choices.

dialogue.greeting: You made it to the shop. Pull up. There’s work on the lift and a story behind most of it.

topics.label: What makes this the home spot?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Everybody on this block sends people here.

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Because a vehicle still has to work after somebody finishes talking about it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the people?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Same problem, harder diagnosis. Majid checks the plan. Gunny asks who actually agreed to it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you do?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Try to build something I can stand behind when the noise dies down.

topics.label: What is behind Mr. Lock Changer?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That tablet story sounds different depending on who is telling it.

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Exactly. My service work is one thing. My cousin got a tablet from me and made his own choices with it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So the police anxiety belongs to another angle too?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Keep your eyes on who is holding the tool and what job they’re really doing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Same object, different intentions.

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: And the joke gets darker when somebody thinks looking like the business means doing the business.

topics.label: Tell me about the van run.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You really lived out of a van while flipping it?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: That G20 got me through a stretch. Michigan, down to Georgia, back up. Making gas money as I went.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And then the green van?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Different vehicle. A lead from the G20 turned into the Econoline sale. Keep those two deals straight.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you have the whole timeline?

lines.speaker: McCluster
lines.text: Pieces. Photos will help put the dates back where they belong. The road stays vivid even when the numbers need checking.

dialogue.farewell: Stay a minute if you need to. Just don’t promise the next job before you hear the whole situation.

garageCrew.name: Majid
garageCrew.role: Garage regular, advisor, and roadside story contact
garageCrew.backstory: Majid is an existing Whip Equipped character whose role includes advising independent money before an exit from the criminal entanglement. The owner’s road recollections also identify him as a supportive voice during the lean van-driving period, while his brother helped tow the earlier camper. This city version uses those established roles without inventing a birthplace, age, mechanic’s qualification, or historical transaction record. He can be funny and skeptical in the garage, but the point of his presence is continuity: the person supporting the protagonist on the road is available when another big plan arrives. New city dialogue dramatizes that relationship. It does not upgrade approximate recollections into verified costs or use legitimate flips as corroboration of fictional crime.
garageCrew.personality: Steady, candid, supportive; asks how a plan works when the excitement wears off.

dialogue.greeting: What’s the plan, and what’s the plan if the first plan eats all the gas money?

topics.label: What were those roadside calls like?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: McCluster says you were on the phone through the van run.

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: You stay with your people when the road starts feeling bigger than the plan.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Were you giving directions?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Sometimes. Sometimes you just need another voice while you figure out the next stop.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Sounds like a lot of uncertainty.

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: It was. Don’t edit that out just because the flip eventually has a selling price.

topics.label: What counts as a good flip?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Buy cheap, sell higher. Simple, right?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Then remember the tow, the gas, the flight, the days, and the ride home.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: McCluster has rough numbers for those.

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Rough numbers are a place to start. Let the records help before you call it exact profit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What matters beyond the number?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Whether you can make the next move without somebody owning the decision for you.

topics.label: Why keep talking about independent money?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why not leave a bad arrangement as soon as you hate it?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Because wanting out and being able to stand on your own are different problems.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So wait forever?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: No. Build the way out while you can still choose what it looks like.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And if somebody keeps changing the terms?

lines.speaker: Majid
lines.text: Then stop confusing their next promise with your own plan.

dialogue.farewell: Check in when you get there. A successful deal includes the trip home.

garageCrew.name: Gunny
garageCrew.backstory: Gunny is the existing story character whose commitments protect autonomy over crews and decisions. The city assigns him a practical point of contact at the garage without inventing an earlier technical career or making him the unconfirmed mechanic behind every repair. He listens to requests, asks who is available, and refuses to treat another person’s time as already promised. That makes him useful in a district where almost every business is advertising more certainty than it possesses. His new conversations connect a funny booking dispute to the story’s more serious concern with who controls a person’s labor and choices. His age, origin, and precise appearance remain unresolved rather than receiving biographical filler.
garageCrew.personality: Direct, grounded, wry; values a clear commitment and the freedom to make it.

dialogue.greeting: Tell me what needs doing. Then we’ll find out who actually agreed to do it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you send your people to help with a shoot?

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: I can ask people. Start there.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I thought you handled the crew.

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: Handling a schedule doesn’t make somebody mine.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So what do you need?

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: The job, the time, the pay, and enough room for somebody to answer honestly.

topics.label: What is wrong with this block’s bookings?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Three shops promised the same van.

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: Did any of them talk to the person holding the keys?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: They talked to each other.

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: Then they built a very confident conversation around an absent vehicle.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How do we fix it?

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: Start with Beatrice. The keys usually have a better understanding of the schedule than the advertisement.

topics.label: What does standing on business mean here?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Everybody keeps saying they stand on business.

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: Then ask what happens when the promise gets inconvenient.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s when you find out?

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: That’s when the slogan has to put shoes on.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the shop?

lines.speaker: Gunny
lines.text: We’ve got enough work without making somebody else’s choice for them. Be clear about what you’re committing to.

dialogue.farewell: If the plan changes, tell the people carrying it.

expansionNeighborhoods.name: The Original Block
expansionNeighborhoods.lore: Harbor Boulevard’s two facing rows: the tea counter, Hordash, Mike Hawk’s campaign office, Robbery 1s, Hitman Gear, RealCameraMen, PressureTV and Baddies on Wheels, with the Whip Equipped garage behind the north row. Everything that follows was built around it, mostly without permits. It is the part of town that still works, which locals find suspicious.

expansionNeighborhoods.name: Bridgefoot Quay
expansionNeighborhoods.lore: The waterfront where the HQ bridge touches the mainland. Developers rebranded it twice in one year and both new names are still printed on the same bus shelter. It has the best view of the Equity Uprise building on its island and the worst parking in the city. The quay is where hustles come to look legitimate: a bail bondsman with a prayer candle in the window, a chicken spot whose sauce has a waiver, a tire shop that also sells sushi, and Thugged Out Apparel, the most expensive “street” clothing ever sold to men who own a boat.

expansionNeighborhoods.name: Precinct Square
expansionNeighborhoods.lore: The city’s civic heart, in the sense that something is technically beating. The Bridgeport Police Department’s headquarters holds one corner under its own name; everything around it is private enterprise with ambitions. St. Copay’s, a private hospital, measures its emergency-room wait in fiscal quarters. The church shares a parking lot with the bank, a sermon schedule with the bank’s overdraft calendar, and a boot technician with Bail Mary’s expediting desk. The School of Hard Knocks sits behind an ivy-covered wall it imported from a richer city, and directly across the square, in a former dentist’s office, Wiggers Anonymous meets every night with fresh coffee and very low expectations.

expansionNeighborhoods.name: Cul-de-Sadness
expansionNeighborhoods.lore: Ten households on curving streets that were supposed to become a golf community until the golf course became a retention pond. Three enormous houses at the end of the loop belong to families who send their sons to the School of Hard Knocks; seven ordinary houses belong to people who work at the hospital, the church and the shops, and who are tired of having their recycling bins tagged with the words BOND ST WILLY WHACKERS in very neat handwriting. The neighborhood’s teenagers go to Harding High School on Bond Street, the real public high school the Willy Whackers have decided to “study.”

expansionNeighborhoods.name: Rustbucket Wharf
expansionNeighborhoods.lore: The industrial harbor on the far side of the city’s working waterfront: cranes nobody operates, a laundromat with an unusually clean cash flow, a car wash that returns most of its cars, a self-storage complex where several units have mailboxes, a pawn shop that buys gold teeth, a motel that rents by the hour and judges by the minute, and the regional headquarters of an essential-oil pyramid with three employees and nine thousand executives. Whip Equipped knows every driveway here and pretends not to.

ads: Hi, my name is Todd. It has been 2,211 days.
Meetings nightly. Bring your legal name.
Your mom called. She wants her son back.
expansionBusinesses.name: Wiggers Anonymous
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Hi, my name is Todd, and it has been 2,211 days since I called anybody “fam.”
expansionBusinesses.description: A recovery fellowship for suburban white guys who built their whole personality out of a cartoon of Black and hip-hop culture they learned from a music video and a gas-station energy drink. Folding chairs, burnt coffee, a donated whiteboard, and a sign-in sheet where half the members still write their rap names.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Gordon Pfeiffer founded the group after the night he tried to settle a homeowners’-association dispute with a freestyle, lost, and was asked by his own daughter to “please just be a dentist.” He was once one. So were Todd and Derek. The three of them rent the old dental office on Precinct Square, still with the reclining chair, and run meetings seven nights a week. The rules are simple: you introduce yourself by your legal name, you surrender one accessory per milestone, and nobody is allowed to describe a personal problem as “the streets” if the problem is a parking ticket in a cul-de-sac. The program does not target anybody’s culture. It targets four grown men who keep mistaking somebody else’s culture for a costume, and one man the School of Hard Knocks pays to stay that way.
expansionBusinesses.memberNote: The owner asked for three suffering members and then named four jobs (drug dealer, Hitman, Equity Uprise, Thugged Out Apparel). The fellowship has four, one per job; Gordon calls the fourth chair “the overflow.”
twelveSteps: We admitted we were powerless over the bass, and that our lives had become a mixtape nobody asked for.
Came to believe that a Power greater than ourselves, usually our mothers’ disappointment, could restore us to khakis.
Made a decision to turn our wardrobe over to the care of someone who has met us.
Made a searching and fearless inventory of our hats.
Admitted to the group and to one other human being the exact nature of our street name.
Were entirely ready to have our legal names restored.
Humbly asked our barber to remove our shortcomings, and the lightning bolt.
Made a list of all persons we had called “bro” in a voice that was not ours, and became willing to apologize to them all.
Made direct amends wherever possible, except when doing so would require another freestyle.
Continued to take personal inventory, and when we said “deadass,” promptly admitted it.
Sought through quiet reflection to improve our conscious contact with our actual hometown.
Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to other guys in cargo shorts and a durag, and to practice these principles in all our group chats.

interior.style: Former dental office with folding chairs and a reclining confession chair
interior.description: A circle of folding chairs, a coffee urn, a whiteboard of anniversary dates, and a donation bin full of surrendered chains, flat-brim hats and one keytar.

ads: Thugged Out Apparel. Street-certified. Yacht-approved.
NEW: hoodies distressed by a licensed therapist.
Now hiring: someone who has been outside.
expansionBusinesses.name: Thugged Out Apparel
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Street-certified. Yacht-approved. Machine wash cold.
expansionBusinesses.description: A boutique that sells pre-ripped hoodies at four hundred credits to men whose only street experience is the one their gated community is named after. The clothes are stitched in the same factory as golf polos and the price tags have their own security guard.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Marty Feldstein spent thirty years selling pastel golf shirts to country clubs. Then a trend consultant told him the money was in “authenticity,” so he bought a waterfront storefront, a fog machine and a font. Thugged Out Apparel has never once been visited by anybody it claims to be inspired by; its customers are hedge-fund dads, School of Hard Knocks parents buying uniforms for their sons’ fake gang, and Hunter, who works the floor on commission and spends every check in the store. Nour, the only employee who can operate the register, keeps the place solvent and keeps a private spreadsheet titled “Things Marty Should Not Say Out Loud.” The satire is the store: culture flattened into a price tag and sold back to the people least entitled to it.

interior.style: Gallery-lit boutique with a fog machine and a velvet rope around one pair of socks
interior.description: Hoodies hang one per wall like paintings. A glass case holds a single sock. A framed trend report explains the brand to the brand.

ads: Sow a seed. Reap a sedan.
Drive-through blessings 9 to 5. Card or cash.

expansionBusinesses.name: Greater Prosperity Tabernacle of the Holy Upsell
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Sow a seed. Reap a sedan.
expansionBusinesses.description: A megachurch in a former mattress showroom, with a fog machine borrowed from Thugged Out Apparel, a tap-to-tithe card reader on every pew, and a sermon series titled “Blessed and Leveraged.”
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Pastor Chad Ledger came to the city with a guitar, a ring light and a theology that fits on a vanity plate. He bought the mattress showroom because it was already zoned for financing. Mother Odessa Pike, who has belonged to every congregation that has ever met on Precinct Square, came with the building and runs the collection plate like a central bank. Half the block attends for different reasons: Beatrice Cole for Mother Odessa, Mike Hawk for whatever service has a camera, Mara Costa only on Easter to run the tea table, Frank Mulrooney for the front pew he has never once paid for, Hollis Ashby for the tax receipt, Linda Babbitt because she is the church secretary, Tammy Pruitt to sell oils in the lobby, Marty Feldstein because he is trying to buy pew sponsorship, Raymond Dupree to “keep my receipts holy,” and Ray Fitch because half his bail clients are in the second row.

Now enrolling: adversity, starting at the low price of everything.
Ask about our Being Robbed practicum.
expansionBusinesses.name: The School of Hard Knocks
expansionBusinesses.category: Private academy, grades 9–12, tuition available on request (do not request)
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Est. last spring. Experience the struggle, fully accredited.
expansionBusinesses.description: The most prestigious, most liberal-arts, most expensive private high school in the city, whose signature program teaches rich kids “the Black experience” as a curriculum, taught entirely by people who have never had it. Coursework includes Authentic Adversity, Code-Switching for Legacy Admissions, and a field practicum in being robbed.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Headmaster Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell founded the academy after an admissions consultant told him colleges wanted “narratives of hardship” and he realized his donors’ children had none. So he built one and charged for it. The ivy on the wall is imported. The “street” out front is private property. The school pays Bryce Lundqvist, a Wiggers Anonymous dropout, a full salary with dental to stand at the gate as the Experiential Adversity Facilitator and shake the students down for lunch money, which is then itemized back onto the tuition bill. The students formed a gang as an extracurricular and named it the Bond Street Willy Whackers, after the street beside Harding High School, the real public school they go to “study.” The school put Bryce in charge of it. They tag its bike racks in calligraphy and “rob” its students of things their parents already bought them twice. The satire’s target is exactly this: a school and a class of rich kids who turned other people’s lives into enrichment programming. The joke is never on the people they think they are studying.
curriculum: Authentic Adversity I & II (honors section requires a minor injury, which the nurse will simulate)
Field Practicum: Being Robbed (graded on vulnerability)
Comparative Hardship (pass/fail; nobody has ever failed)
Gentrification Studies, taught on location while touring properties the board owns

interior.style: Mahogany lobby, imported ivy and a trophy case of hardship certificates
interior.description: A wood-panelled lobby, a donor wall, a framed photo of the founding class pretending to be in a gang, and a sign that says this campus is a safe space for narratives.

expansionBusinesses.name: Harding High School
expansionBusinesses.category: Public high school, Bridgeport Public Schools
expansionBusinesses.tagline: 379 Bond Street, Bridgeport, Connecticut
expansionBusinesses.description: Bridgeport’s public high school on Bond Street, in a building that opened in 2018 on the site of a former General Electric plant. The Bond Street Willy Whackers from the School of Hard Knocks come here to “study” its students, who are mostly just trying to get through chemistry.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy teaches history and coaches debate here, and her students win tournaments against academies with planetariums. The Willy Whackers roll down Bond Street after their practicum to “rob” her students of phones their parents are still paying off, then return them with a handwritten reflection essay. Dr. Abernathy writes up every incident for the boys’ headmaster and the police records window. Her daughter Imani keeps a separate archive, and it is better organized than the headmaster’s.

expansionBusinesses.description: A private hospital with a charity name. The emergency-room wait is measured in fiscal quarters, the vending machine sells aspirin by the half-tablet, and the cosmetic wing is nicer than the cardiology wing because cosmetic pays up front.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: St. Copay’s was a charity hospital until a private-equity firm bought it, renamed the chapel the Revenue Cycle Center, and installed a card reader on the defibrillator. Charge nurse Rosa Delgado holds the emergency room together with tape, sarcasm and a personal stash of saline. Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff runs the cosmetic emergency department, which treats crises like asymmetric lip filler, and is the hospital’s most profitable physician. Bail Mary’s expediting desk sells “priority intake” wristbands in the waiting room. The emergency room does not recognize them, and Rosa keeps the confiscated ones in a jar.

expansionBusinesses.category: Bail bonds, devotional candles and a back-counter “expediting” desk
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Hail Mary, full of bail.
expansionBusinesses.description: A bail-bond office with prayer candles in the window, a confession booth that doubles as a payment kiosk, a lifetime-customer loyalty card, and at the back counter Mulrooney & Son Expediting, a family fixer desk with a laminated menu.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Ray Fitch is a Tabernacle deacon who realized his congregation and his clientele were the same people on different days. He sells bonds Monday through Saturday and forgiveness on Sunday, and he has a combo package. He rents the back counter to Frank Mulrooney, whose Mulrooney & Son Expediting promises to make tickets, files and competitors “go away” and has never once reached anybody who could. Frank refers clients to Ray for a cut; Ray refers them back for a cut of the cut. Brenda Szabo laminated the menu. Dale Pruitt boots cars in the lot the church shares with the bank and takes the removal fee.

interior.description: A counter, a confession booth payment kiosk, a wall of devotional candles with prices on the bottom, and a back counter with a laminated menu, a tip jar and a shredder labeled ARCHIVE.

Today’s hottest sauce: Tuition.
expansionBusinesses.name: Wing Stop Crying
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Our sauce makes grown men cry. So does our health inspection.
expansionBusinesses.description: A wing shop whose hottest sauce requires a signed waiver, a witness and a notary from the hookah lounge next door.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Sami Haddad opened the shop with his family recipe and a modest sauce. Then the Willy Whackers started daring each other to eat the hot one and posting the results as “hardship content,” so Sami made it hotter every week out of spite. The current sauce is called Tuition. St. Copay’s has a dedicated intake form for it.

interior.description: A fryer line, a heat-level chart that ends in a drawing of a gravestone, and a waiver desk with a pen on a chain.

expansionBusinesses.name: Sushi & Tire Center
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Raw fish. Retreads. One fridge.
expansionBusinesses.description: A tire shop that started serving sushi because the walk-in cooler was already there. Rotations come with miso. Nobody has asked which side of the cooler is which.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Gus Pappas has changed tires on Bridgefoot Quay for forty years and learned sushi from a television series during a slow winter. The lunch combo is a California roll and a rotation. He has excellent online reviews from people who were too scared to leave bad ones.

interior.style: Tire bay with a sushi bar
interior.description: Two lifts, a stack of tires, a six-seat sushi counter and one shared cooler with a strip of tape down the middle.

expansionBusinesses.description: A hookah lounge whose owner is a commissioned notary. Leases, affidavits and Wing Stop Crying waivers are stamped between flavors.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Tobias Lund got his notary commission to make his lounge sound more legitimate and accidentally became the city’s busiest notary. He has notarized three marriages, two divorces and a pinky promise. His stamp smells like mint.

interior.description: Low couches, hookahs, and a notary desk with a stamp, an ink pad and a fire extinguisher.

expansionBusinesses.tagline: Fees on fees on fees.
expansionBusinesses.description: A bank whose fee schedule is longer than the city charter. It charges for deposits, withdrawals, looking at the ATM and being told about the fees.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Branch manager Whitney Crane earns a bonus for every fee and has invented four this year, including the Feeling Fee. The bank shares a parking lot with the Tabernacle, and Pastor Ledger times his offering appeals to payday direct deposits.

interior.description: Teller windows, velvet ropes that loop back on themselves, and a fee schedule bound like a family Bible.

ads: Biggest refund in town or I do the time. Again.
expansionBusinesses.name: Refund Raymond’s Tax Prep
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Biggest refund in town or I do the time. Again.
expansionBusinesses.description: A tax office run by a man audited six times, proudly framed on the wall in chronological order.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Raymond Dupree promises the biggest refund in the city and has kept the promise by inventing deductions with confidence. He claims the church, the hookah lounge and the Willy Whackers as dependents for certain clients. He has done the time twice and says the third time is for the brand.

interior.style: Strip-mall tax office
interior.description: A desk, a calculator taped to the desk, and six framed audit letters.

ads: Mild Violence Tag & Title: Take a number.
Now serving: 19.
expansionBusinesses.name: Mild Violence Tag & Title Express
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Take a number. Take a seat. Take a hint.
expansionBusinesses.description: A private registration-renewal shop decorated to look like a motor-vehicles office, renamed by its own customers after a fistfight over a vision chart that was only there for atmosphere. Twelve windows, one open. The take-a-number dispenser is on 4,000 and serving 19.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Gloria Benitez has staffed Window 3 for thirty-one years and outlasted five owners, two buildings and a fire. She is the only employee, the other eleven windows are painted on, and the shop charges a convenience fee to stand in its line instead of somebody else’s. She takes her lunch at a different time every day so nobody can plan around it.

interior.style: Twelve windows, eleven painted on
interior.description: A take-a-number dispenser, a row of plastic chairs bolted together, and eleven very realistic paintings of closed windows.

ads: Side Effects Pharmacy. Ask your doctor if your doctor is right for you.
expansionBusinesses.name: Side Effects Pharmacy
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Ask your doctor if your doctor is right for you.
expansionBusinesses.description: A pharmacy whose receipts are so long they are sold as scarves in winter, and whose pharmacist reads every side effect out loud whether or not you asked.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD, believes in informed consent so completely that it takes him forty minutes to hand over a cough drop. St. Copay’s sends patients to him because he is the only person in the city who will explain their bill.

interior.style: Pharmacy counter with a receipt printer the size of a loom
interior.description: Shelves of remedies, a counseling window and a receipt printer that never stops.

ads: Spin Cycle: We clean everything.
Open 24 hours. Revenue 25.
expansionBusinesses.name: Spin Cycle Laundromat & Money Laundering
expansionBusinesses.tagline: We clean everything. Don’t ask what.
expansionBusinesses.description: A twenty-four-hour laundromat with forty machines, three customers and the highest reported revenue per square foot in the state.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Lou Baranski bought the laundromat with money he describes as “found,” and the machines have reported a profit every single quarter, including the quarter they were unplugged. Refund Raymond does his books. Frank Mulrooney’s expediting desk does his “security,” in the sense that Frank picks up an envelope every Friday and does nothing.

interior.style: Rows of washers with an unusually busy back office
interior.description: Washers and dryers, a change machine, and a back-office door marked LINT.

ads: Joyride: We wash it. We drive it.
Usually we bring it back.
expansionBusinesses.name: Joyride Hand Car Wash
expansionBusinesses.tagline: We wash it. We drive it. Usually we bring it back.
expansionBusinesses.description: A hand car wash whose detail service includes a test drive nobody requested. Cars come back cleaner, warmer and with a different radio station.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Dante Moreau loves cars more than he loves the concept of asking. Every car that comes through Joyride gets a full wash and “a quick spin to dry it.” The quick spin has included the highway twice. Whip Equipped will not let him near the garage’s lift, and Dante considers this the highest compliment in town.

interior.style: Wash tunnel and a key board with suspicious gaps
interior.description: Hoses, buckets, a wall of hooks for customer keys and a whiteboard of mileage that does not add up.

ads: U-Hide: Residents strictly prohibited.
Ask Earl. He’s home.
expansionBusinesses.name: U-Hide Self Storage
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Units from 49 credits. Residents strictly prohibited (wink).
expansionBusinesses.description: A self-storage complex where several units have doormats, one has a satellite dish, and the manager lives in 14B.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Earl Pickens has managed U-Hide for twenty years and lived in it for nineteen. He enforces the no-residents rule strictly, against everyone except himself and the tenant in 22A, who makes good soup. His unit has a porch light.

interior.style: Front office with a key cabinet and a very lived-in back hallway
interior.description: A sales counter, a wall of padlocks for sale and a hallway smell of soup.

ads: Kash 4 Gold Teeth. We do not ask whose.
expansionBusinesses.name: Kash 4 Gold Teeth Pawn
expansionBusinesses.tagline: We buy gold. We buy teeth. We do not ask whose.
expansionBusinesses.description: A pawn shop whose glass cases contain six hundred watches that stopped at different times, a high-school debate trophy that Norma refuses to sell, and an entire tray of gold teeth.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Norma Klein has run the pawn shop since the ferry stopped. She appraises everything with a jeweler’s loupe and a facial expression. The Willy Whackers try to pawn their fathers’ watches every month as part of their practicum, and Norma calls their fathers every month.

interior.style: Pawn counter behind bars
interior.description: Glass cases, a buzzer door, a tray of teeth and a high-school debate trophy with a NOT FOR SALE tag.

ads: The No-Tell Motel. Hourly rates. Daily regrets.
expansionBusinesses.name: The No-Tell Motel
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Hourly rates. Daily regrets.
expansionBusinesses.description: A two-story motel where every guest is registered as Mr. and Mrs. Smith and the ice machine has seen things.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Patti Larkin runs the front desk and has never once told anybody anything, which is why everybody in the city tells her everything. She knows which councilman is in room 9 and which deacon is in room 11 and she will take both to her grave, unless the price is right.

interior.style: Wood-panelled front desk and a bell nobody rings
interior.description: A front desk behind plexiglass, a key board, an ice machine and a guest book where every name is Smith.

ads: Uplineage. Be your own boss’s boss’s boss.
Ask me about financial freedom (please).
expansionBusinesses.name: Uplineage Essential Oils
expansionBusinesses.tagline: Be your own boss’s boss’s boss.
expansionBusinesses.description: The regional headquarters of an essential-oil opportunity with three employees and nine thousand Diamond Executive Founders.
expansionBusinesses.backstory: Kayleigh Spurlock is a Diamond Executive Platinum Founder, which means she recruited Tammy Pruitt, who recruited the entire Bail Mary Bombers softball team. The oils are mostly lavender. The business model is mostly Tammy. Kayleigh has a car the company technically owns and a garage full of inventory she technically bought.

interior.style: Pastel office with a vision board
interior.description: Shelves of tiny bottles, a ring light, a recruitment pyramid labeled TEAM TREE, and a closet of unsold starter kits.

expansionNpcs.name: Gordon Pfeiffer
expansionNpcs.role: Founder and meeting chair, Wiggers Anonymous (formerly “Lil Mortgage”)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Gordon was a periodontist with a boat, a gold grill he had made in his own office, and a SoundCloud page with eleven listeners, nine of them patients. He called himself Lil Mortgage. The bottom came at a homeowners’-association meeting, where he tried to win a fence-height dispute with a freestyle, lost the dispute, lost the vote and lost his daughter’s respect in one sixteen-bar verse. She asked him to please just be a dentist. He has been clean since June 2, 2014. He closed the practice, kept the reclining chair, and turned the office into the meeting room. He is gentle, relentless and completely unimpressed by anybody’s origin story, including his own. I was once one, he says, and then he makes you take the hat off.
expansionNpcs.personality: Patient, dry, unshockable; a former performer who now treats every performance as a symptom.

dialogue.greeting: Come in. Coffee’s burnt, chairs are folding, and you’ll introduce yourself with your legal name.

topics.label: What do you mean, “I was once one”?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Were you really one of them?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Lil Mortgage. Three mixtapes, all burned to disc, all handed out at a dental conference.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What changed?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: I tried to win a fence dispute with a freestyle. The fence won. So did my daughter’s look.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And now?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Now I hand out chips and take hats. Two thousand days of saying “thank you” in my own voice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How’s the group this month?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Gary thinks oregano is a business model. Brett thinks a light stand is a weapon. Logan thinks a delivery route is a turf.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And Hunter?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Hunter gets paid in the costume. That’s the hardest kind. The store is the relapse.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Any progress?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Logan used his real name at the front desk on the island. We cried. Todd brought a cake.

topics.label: What about the guy at the school gate?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There’s a guy outside the private school who looks like your target market.

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Bryce. He came to three meetings, then the School of Hard Knocks offered him dental.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: They pay him to stay like that?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Salary, dental and a title: Experiential Adversity Facilitator. It is the most expensive relapse in the city.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Can you reach him?

lines.speaker: Gordon Pfeiffer
lines.text: Not while somebody is paying for the costume. You can’t recover from a job description.

dialogue.farewell: Keep coming back. Leave the chain in the bin.

expansionNpcs.name: Todd Brenneman
expansionNpcs.role: Sponsor and street outreach, Wiggers Anonymous (formerly “T-Bizzle Brenneman”)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Todd sold timeshares and introduced himself to every client with a handshake that had nine stages. He had a vanity plate, a backwards visor and a speech pattern he picked up from a basketball video game. His wife left him a note that said “I married a Todd.” He has been clean 2,211 days and he announces the number to strangers. Now he walks the city in khakis and a fleece vest, doing gentle interventions on any grown man in cargo shorts and a durag. He sponsors Logan and Hunter. He is extremely proud of his khakis, which he describes as “the uniform of recovery.”
expansionNpcs.personality: Earnest, loud, a reformed salesman now selling sobriety with the same handshake.

dialogue.greeting: Hi. My name is Todd, and it has been 2,211 days since I called anybody fam.

topics.label: What are you doing out here?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why are you following that man in the visor?

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: Outreach. He just said “no cap” to a parking meter. That’s a cry for help.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you say to him?

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: I tell him my name. My real one. Then I let the silence do the work.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does it work?

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: Once. Usually he calls me “unc.” Which, honestly, hurts more than it should.

topics.label: You sponsor the guy at Thugged Out Apparel?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Isn’t your sponsee working in a store that sells the costume?

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: Hunter. It’s like an alcoholic tending bar, except the bar costs four hundred credits a hoodie.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why not quit?

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: Commission. He made eight hundred last week and spent nine hundred in the same store.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s bad math.

lines.speaker: Todd Brenneman
lines.text: Nour told him that. He called her “shorty.” She charged him a restocking fee for it.

dialogue.farewell: Khakis are a choice. Choose them.

expansionNpcs.name: Derek Vollmer
expansionNpcs.role: Literature table and walking pamphleteer, Wiggers Anonymous (formerly “Yung Mayo”)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Derek was Yung Mayo, a name he chose without irony and defended in a public comment section for three years. He was a mid-level insurance adjuster who spent his weekends filming music videos in a rented car he could not afford. He hit bottom when PressureTV aired one of the videos on a segment called “What Is This.” Now he walks a pamphlet route past both high schools, because he believes the earlier the intervention, the better. He leaves pamphlets on the School of Hard Knocks gate; Bryce uses them as napkins. Derek has a very calm voice he practiced for a year to replace the old one.
expansionNpcs.personality: Soft-spoken, tidy, painfully sincere; uses pamphlets the way other people use small talk.

dialogue.greeting: Pamphlet? It’s called “So You Gave Yourself a Nickname.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is it true you were called Yung Mayo?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: I was going for confident. I landed on condiment.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How long did you go by it?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: Three years, two cars and one PressureTV segment called “What Is This.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you miss it?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: Sometimes, at a sandwich counter. Then I read page four.

topics.label: Why walk past the high schools?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why is your route past both schools?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: Prevention. The private-school kids are pre-symptomatic. Their school is paying for the symptoms.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the public-school kids?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: They don’t need pamphlets. They need the private-school kids to stop stealing their calculators.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do the rich kids read them?

lines.speaker: Derek Vollmer
lines.text: Graham did. He asked if recovery counts toward community-service hours. It does not.

dialogue.farewell: Read page four. Page four is the one that got me.

expansionNpcs.name: Gary Babbitt
expansionNpcs.role: Wiggers Anonymous member; “pharmaceutical entrepreneur” (sells oregano)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Gary lives in his mother’s basement in Cul-de-Sadness and calls it the trap. He calls himself G-Babb$ and says he is a drug dealer, which would be serious if anything he sold were a drug. His supplier is the spice aisle. His bestseller is oregano. His premium product is loose tea he buys retail at GAURANFUCKING TEA and resells in sandwich bags at a loss. Nobody has ever arrested him, because nothing in the bag is illegal, so every month he pays Frank Mulrooney’s laminated-menu price at Bail Mary to keep it that way, out of respect for the process. His mother, Linda, prays for him by name at the Tabernacle. He comes to Wiggers Anonymous because she drives him. He has three days.
expansionNpcs.personality: Self-important, broke, deeply loyal to his mom; the least dangerous dealer in America.

workplace.description: Calls himself a drug dealer. Sells oregano, basil and Gauranfucking Tea leaves in sandwich bags.

dialogue.greeting: You looking? I got that loud. It’s oregano. It’s very loud oregano.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s in the bag?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Premium Mediterranean. Very potent. Very aromatic.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It’s oregano.

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Keep your voice down. My margins depend on the mystery.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do people buy it?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Gus at the sushi place buys it for the miso. Repeat customer. That’s a plug, technically.

topics.label: Aren’t you worried about the police?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Doesn’t anybody arrest you?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Never. It’s oregano. So I pay Frank Mulrooney to keep it that way.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Keep what that way?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: The not-arresting. Twenty credits, laminated menu. I like to support local institutions.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You pay a fixer to fix nothing?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: It’s about respect. Also Mom says I should always tip.

topics.label: Why do you go to Wiggers Anonymous?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You go to the meetings?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Mom drives me. She waits in the lot with the engine running so I can’t walk home.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is it helping?

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Three days. I said “hello” to a cop in my real voice yesterday. It felt like being naked.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds like progress.

lines.speaker: Gary Babbitt
lines.text: Gordon said that. Then he took my hat. I had that hat since I was twenty-nine.

dialogue.farewell: Stay safe out here. Mom says the casserole’s at six.

expansionNpcs.name: Brett Sorensen
expansionNpcs.role: Wiggers Anonymous member; equipment runner at Hitman Gear (thinks it is an assassin supplier)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Brett applied to Hitman Gear because of the name. He believed for six full weeks that it supplied contract killers, and he called every light stand “the choppa” until Vik Rao gently explained it was a light stand. Vik keeps him on a trial basis because Brett is genuinely good at carrying heavy things to the right room, provided nobody tells him which room is a “mission.” At night he plays the PRIM3 tactical game and describes it to the group as training. He goes by The Hitman, a name nobody at the shop uses, especially Owen, who calls him Brett in a voice so kind it ends conversations.
expansionNpcs.personality: Enthusiastic, gullible, physically helpful; treats every errand like a briefing.

dialogue.greeting: Target acquired. Sorry. I mean: hello. Gordon says I have to say hello.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you do at Hitman Gear?

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: Heavy extraction. Of sandbags. To the van.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You know it’s a film-equipment shop?

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: Vik told me in week six. I took it hard. I had already bought gloves.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Are you staying?

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: The gloves are good for C-stands. Owen says I have a future in grip. I said grip what. He said grip.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The group says you call a video game your training.

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: Tactical simulation. Turn-based. I clear rooms at night.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Has it helped your real life?

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: I cleared a room at Hitman Gear. It was the break room. Marisol was eating lunch.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How did that go?

lines.speaker: Brett Sorensen
lines.text: She finished her sandwich while I apologized. That’s my nineteenth day, actually. That apology.

dialogue.farewell: I’m going dark. That means I’m going home.

expansionNpcs.name: Logan Pemberton
expansionNpcs.role: Wiggers Anonymous member; contract courier on the Equity Uprise HQ delivery run
expansionNpcs.backstory: Logan is a trust-fund kid who took a courier contract delivering packages across the bridge to the Equity Uprise HQ front desk, because he heard the word Equity and assumed it meant he was getting some. He calls his delivery route “my block,” the bridge “the trap bridge” and his bicycle “the whip,” which the Whip Equipped crew has asked him to stop doing. Logan grew up with a sailboat and a polo pony and describes his childhood as “coming up.” His milestone this month: he signed the HQ delivery log with his legal name for the first time. Todd cried. Logan is forty-one days clean and still has the visor in his bag, just in case.
expansionNpcs.personality: Polished, oblivious, cheerful; mistakes privilege for a backstory and a route for a turf.

workplace.role: Contract courier; drops packages at the HQ front desk and leaves

dialogue.greeting: Package for the front desk. I mean: hi. I’m Logan. Legal name. Forty-one days.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You work on the island?

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: Contract courier. I bring boxes across the bridge to the front desk and then I leave.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you get equity?

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: I asked. Twice. The second time, the person at the desk just handed me a pen and the delivery log.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: I signed Logan Pemberton. Not L-Dawg. First time ever. Todd brought a cake to the meeting.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Gordon says you talk about “coming up.”

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: Greenwich. It was rough. The polo pony was on a payment plan.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s not rough.

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: That’s what step eleven is about. Conscious contact with my actual hometown.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How is that going?

lines.speaker: Logan Pemberton
lines.text: I can say Greenwich without making it sound like a threat now. Progress.

dialogue.farewell: Back to the block. The route. My route. Sorry.

expansionNpcs.name: Hunter Gustafson
expansionNpcs.role: Wiggers Anonymous member; floor salesman at Thugged Out Apparel (commission)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Hunter is Thugged Out Apparel’s top salesman and its top customer, which Nour has explained to him is not a business plan. He calls himself Hunnid Hunter. He sells pre-distressed hoodies to hedge-fund dads with total conviction because he believes every word on the tags, which Marty wrote after reading a trend report. Todd sponsors him and visits the store to sit near him in silence. Hunter has relapsed so many times that the group gave him a chip that just says “again.” Today is day zero. He is very excited about day one.
expansionNpcs.personality: Sunny, gullible, devoted to the merchandise; the store is both his job and his relapse.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to Thugged Out. Everything here is certified street. I don’t know who certifies it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What should I buy?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: The pre-distressed hoodie. Each hole is made by a licensed therapist.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why a therapist?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: Marty says it adds narrative. The holes have been through something.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you bought one?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: Four. I’m on commission. Nour says I owe the store money now. Every week I get a little more street.

topics.label: Todd says you’re on day zero.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How many days do you have?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: Zero. Which is the closest number to one.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What happened?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: New drop came in. Golf-club durag. I tried it on to describe it to a customer.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Hunter Gustafson
lines.text: And I described it for six hours. Tomorrow is day one. I’m going to wear a polo. My own polo.

dialogue.farewell: Stay thugged out. Or, Todd says, stay in khakis. Either way, receipts are in the bag.

expansionNpcs.name: Marty Feldstein
expansionNpcs.role: Owner and creative director, Thugged Out Apparel
expansionNpcs.backstory: Marty spent thirty years wholesaling pastel golf shirts. A trend consultant he paid a large sum told him to pivot to authenticity, and Marty heard a product category. He has never once asked anybody whose culture he is selling, because he is worried they will say something that is bad for margins. He describes the store as “a conversation,” although he does all the talking. He is lobbying the Tabernacle to rename pew 4 after the brand. Nour keeps a spreadsheet of things he must not say aloud; it has 214 rows.
expansionNpcs.personality: Salesman to the bone; cheerful, shameless, and allergic to the question of who his brand is about.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome, welcome. Feel the fabric. That’s struggle. Imported struggle.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who exactly is Thugged Out Apparel for?

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: People who want the street without the inconvenience of the street.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you ever been to the street?

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: I own the storefront on it. That’s a deeper relationship, legally.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who buys this stuff?

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: Hedge-fund guys, private-school parents and Hunter. Hunter is a loyalty program with legs.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Nour seems to run everything.

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: Nour is our compliance department, finance department and conscience. I pay her as a cashier.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does she agree with your choices?

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: She has a spreadsheet. I’m not allowed to see it, but she reads me a row every morning.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What was this morning’s?

lines.speaker: Marty Feldstein
lines.text: Row 212: do not describe a hoodie as having “seen things.” The hoodie was made last Thursday.

dialogue.farewell: Tell your friends. Tell their accountants.

expansionNpcs.name: Nour Haddad
expansionNpcs.role: Register and actual management, Thugged Out Apparel
expansionNpcs.backstory: Nour studies accounting at night and is, by every measure, the only adult supervision in Thugged Out Apparel. She took the job because it pays more than the wing counter at her father’s shop and because she wanted to see a business fail in real time for school. It hasn’t failed, entirely because of her. She keeps a 214-row spreadsheet of things Marty must not say, charges Hunter a restocking fee every time he calls her shorty, and refuses to sell anything to the Willy Whackers without a parent’s card and a written apology to the student they took it from.
expansionNpcs.personality: Dry, exact, unbothered; quietly the most competent person on the waterfront.

dialogue.greeting: Hi. The hoodie is 140 credits. It is worth eleven. Do you still want it?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s this famous spreadsheet?

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: Things Marty should not say out loud. Two hundred and fourteen rows.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Read me one.

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: Row 98: do not tell a customer the fog machine is “for atmosphere, like a block party.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does he follow it?

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: He follows it like Hunter follows the program. Enthusiastically and for about a day.

topics.label: Do the Willy Whackers shop here?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do the private-school kids come in?

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: Every Friday. They want the varsity hoodies for their gang.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you sell to them?

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: With a parent’s card and a written apology to the kid they robbed. Kensington’s apology was three words.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Which words?

lines.speaker: Nour Haddad
lines.text: “My bad, though.” I made him write it in cursive. His school has a calligraphy requirement.

dialogue.farewell: Keep the receipt. You’ll want it.

expansionNpcs.name: Pastor Chad Ledger
expansionNpcs.role: Senior pastor, Greater Prosperity Tabernacle of the Holy Upsell
expansionNpcs.backstory: Chad came to the city with a guitar, a ring light and a theology that fits on a vanity plate. He bought a closed mattress showroom because it was already zoned for financing and preached his first sermon from a display bed. His series titles read like a car dealership: Blessed and Leveraged, Faith Without Credit Is Dead, Zero Percent Down on Your Destiny. He believes every word, which is what makes him dangerous to his congregation’s checking accounts. Mother Odessa runs his collection plate and is the only person he fears. He drives two sedans and preaches about both.
expansionNpcs.personality: Charismatic, sunny, financially evangelical; earnestly believes prosperity is a spiritual credit score.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome home, friend. Tap to tithe on your way in. Contactless is also a gift.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You keep saying “sow a seed.”

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: A seed is a gift you give in faith, expecting a harvest.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the harvest?

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: For me it was a sedan. For Brittany, also a sedan. The Lord likes a matching set.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And for the congregation?

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: Their harvest is seasonal. Like their payday. Mother Odessa keeps the calendar.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who sits in your pews?

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: Frank Mulrooney, front row. Beatrice from Baddies, Mike Hawk when the cameras are on, Mara at Easter.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do they all believe?

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: Hollis believes in the receipt. Marty believes in pew naming rights. Raymond itemizes communion.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And Linda Babbitt?

lines.speaker: Pastor Chad Ledger
lines.text: Linda believes for all of them. She has a prayer list. Gary is on every line of it.

dialogue.farewell: Go in prosperity. And in the right lane, the left one has a toll.

expansionNpcs.name: Mother Odessa Pike
expansionNpcs.role: Church mother and keeper of the collection plate
expansionNpcs.backstory: Odessa has belonged to every congregation that has ever met on Precinct Square, which has been four churches, a Pentecostal storefront and, for one summer, a yoga studio. She came with the mattress building the way the plumbing did. She runs the collection plate like a central bank, reconciles every service to the cent and is the only reason the Tabernacle has never been audited. She thinks Chad is a good boy with bad ideas. She lets Beatrice Cole sit with her because Beatrice is the only person on the block who can keep up with her on gossip and on the hymns.
expansionNpcs.personality: Formidable, funny, exact; knows every sin in the city by its dollar value and forgives most of them.

dialogue.greeting: Sit up straight. You’re in church, even if it used to sell box springs.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: They say nobody touches the plate but you.

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: Nobody touches the plate but me. Not the pastor, not the deacon, not the card reader.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What about the card reader?

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: I reconcile the card reader by hand. It once tried to round up. We had words.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who won?

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: The Lord and I, in that order. Chad got a new card reader. It is more humble now.

topics.label: Why does Beatrice Cole sit with you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You and Beatrice from Baddies on Wheels seem close.

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: She keeps the keys on her block, I keep the plate on mine. Professional respect.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you talk about?

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: Hymns, and who parked in whose spot. Mostly the second one.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is she here for the faith?

lines.speaker: Mother Odessa Pike
lines.text: She’s here for me. That counts. The Lord takes referrals.

dialogue.farewell: God sees everything. I see the receipts.

expansionNpcs.name: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
expansionNpcs.role: Founding headmaster, The School of Hard Knocks
expansionNpcs.backstory: Winthrop founded the School of Hard Knocks after an admissions consultant told him top colleges wanted “narratives of hardship.” He looked at his donors’ children and saw a market failure. He bought ivy from a richer city, built a wall to hang it on, and hired a curriculum committee in which nobody has experienced anything on the syllabus. He hired Bryce Lundqvist to stand at the gate and extort the students because “authentic adversity cannot be simulated, only outsourced.” Lunch money Bryce collects is itemized back onto tuition as an Adversity Materials Fee. He considers himself a progressive. His donors agree, because he invoices them like one.
expansionNpcs.personality: Polished, condescending, monetizing every word he learned from a diversity seminar he did not attend.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to the School of Hard Knocks. Please mind the ivy, it was very expensive.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What exactly is your curriculum?

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: The Black experience, taught as a rigorous liberal-arts sequence.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who teaches it?

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: A faculty with impeccable credentials and, I’m pleased to say, no personal exposure. It keeps them objective.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds like the opposite of the point.

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: The point is admissions. The point has always been admissions.

topics.label: Why is a grown man extorting your students?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There is an adult at your gate taking students’ money.

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: Mr. Lundqvist, our Experiential Adversity Facilitator. Salaried, with dental.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: He robs children.

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: He facilitates a practicum. The funds return as a line item. It’s a closed loop of growth.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do the parents know?

lines.speaker: Dr. Winthrop Ashcroft-Pell
lines.text: The parents requested it. The waiting list is four hundred families long.

dialogue.farewell: Do consider a gift. Hardship is not cheap.

expansionNpcs.name: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
expansionNpcs.role: Dean of Authenticity, The School of Hard Knocks
expansionNpcs.backstory: Skyler has a master’s degree in Authenticity Studies from a program that no longer exists and the title Dean of Authenticity at a school founded last spring. Skyler leads the Field Practicum, which consists of walking a line of rich kids to the public school so they can “observe,” then to Wing Stop Crying so they can eat the Tuition wings and film themselves suffering for their applications. Skyler apologizes to everyone on the route in advance and then does all of it anyway, which Dr. Abernathy describes as the most expensive way to be useless she has ever seen.
expansionNpcs.personality: Breathy, apologetic, endlessly self-aware and endlessly unchanged.
expansionNpcs.note: Leads the weekly field trip to Bond Street, across from Harding High School, and Wing Stop Crying.

dialogue.greeting: Hi. I want to acknowledge that I’m occupying this sidewalk. Anyway, we’re on a field trip.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Where are you taking these kids?

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: We observe the public school, then we process at Wing Stop Crying.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Observe what?

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: Lived reality. From across the street. We’re not allowed closer since the calculator incident.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What calculator incident?

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: Three of them, actually. Same calculator. Mateo Delgado’s. Kensington keeps “robbing” it for credit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why end the trip at a wing shop?

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: The Tuition sauce produces measurable adversity. The boys film it for their personal essays.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s not adversity. That’s a sauce.

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: I know. I’m aware. I’ve named it in my reflection journal.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will you stop?

lines.speaker: Skyler Moonbeam-Katz
lines.text: Mr. Haddad keeps making it hotter. I think we’re in a dialogue. I think he’s winning.

dialogue.farewell: Thank you for holding space. I didn’t ask, and I’m sorry.

expansionNpcs.name: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
expansionNpcs.role: Experiential Adversity Facilitator (the school’s hired extortionist) and paid leader of the Bond Street Willy Whackers
expansionNpcs.backstory: Bryce is exactly what Wiggers Anonymous was built for, and he knows it. He came to three meetings. On the fourth day the School of Hard Knocks offered him a salary, dental and a title to stand at its gate and shake the students down for lunch money in the costume he was trying to quit. The school itemizes his collections back onto tuition; Bryce gets a W-2. He calls himself B-Rex. He is not a criminal, technically: he is a contractor with a performance review. The school also pays him to lead the boys’ gang, the Bond Street Willy Whackers: he walks them down Bond Street on Tuesdays, holds the calculator they “rob,” and makes sure it goes back on Wednesday with an essay. He is the only adult member, and the only one who has ever read the bylaws to the end. Gordon still saves him a chair. Bryce walks the morning’s collections to Overdraft National Bank and pays the deposit fee, which he considers the only real violence in town.
expansionNpcs.personality: Swaggering, cynical, surprisingly honest about the scam; knows he is a product and resents the price.

group.note: Attended three meetings, then took the school’s job offer.

expansionNpcs.note: Stands at the academy gate; walks to the bank to deposit the morning’s collections.

dialogue.greeting: Lunch money, Chad. Sorry, you’re not Chad. Everybody’s Chad at eight a.m.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The school actually pays you to rob students?

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: Salary, dental and a rubric. I grade them on how convincingly they hand it over.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s insane.

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: Their parents pay forty grand for this. I make thirty-one. Who’s getting robbed?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you feel bad?

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: I feel employed. Gordon says that’s the same feeling wearing a different hat.

topics.label: Why did you leave Wiggers Anonymous?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Gordon says you came to three meetings.

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: Good meetings. Bad coffee. Then a school offered me dental to stay exactly like this.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You could still go back.

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: The day this job ends, I’m in the chair. Until then, I’m a line item.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does anyone know you’re self-aware?

lines.speaker: Bryce “B-Rex” Lundqvist
lines.text: Nour at the clothing store. She sold me khakis last week. I keep them in the trunk.

dialogue.farewell: Gate opens at eight. Bring exact change, it helps your rubric.

expansionNpcs.name: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
expansionNpcs.role: Student, The School of Hard Knocks; founder of the Bond Street Willy Whackers
expansionNpcs.backstory: Tucker founded the Bond Street Willy Whackers, a “gang” named for the street beside Harding High School, which they “study,” and, Tucker insists, for the municipal bonds in his trust. He wrote the bylaws. There are bylaws. He tags the public school’s bike racks in calligraphy, buys his colors at Thugged Out Apparel with his mother’s card, and keeps a reflection journal about the hardships he has scheduled. His sister Sloane, twelve, has read the journal and has notes. He is not dangerous. He is insufferable, and his school is billing for it.
expansionNpcs.personality: Entitled, performative, organized to a fault; mistakes logistics for street credibility.

dialogue.greeting: You know who runs this block? The Bond Street Willy Whackers. We have a charter. It’s laminated.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What are the Bond Street Willy Whackers?

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: The hardest crew in Cul-de-Sadness. Named after Bond Street. And my bonds.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you do?

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: We rob kids at Harding. Then we return everything with a reflection essay. It’s graded.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s just homework.

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: It’s homework with stakes. Kensington got a B-minus. He was devastated.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does your family know about the gang?

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Mom funds it. Dad doesn’t know where I go to school.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And your sister?

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Sloane read my reflection journal. She corrected my grammar and wrote “this is a costume” in the margin.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is she wrong?

lines.speaker: Tucker Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: She’s twelve. She doesn’t understand the struggle. I scheduled mine for Tuesdays.

dialogue.farewell: Don’t tell my mom I was out past the practicum.

expansionNpcs.name: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
expansionNpcs.role: Student, The School of Hard Knocks; self-titled enforcer of the Bond Street Willy Whackers
expansionNpcs.backstory: Kensington gave himself the name K-Murda after losing a fencing match, which is the most violent thing that has ever happened to him. He is the Willy Whackers’ enforcer, a role that consists of taking Mateo Delgado’s calculator every Tuesday and returning it Wednesday with a reflection essay. His father wants to put luxury condos across Bond Street from Harding High School. Kensington wants a tattoo and is not allowed one until his eighteenth birthday, which his mother has already booked at a spa.
expansionNpcs.personality: Loud, nervous, theatrical; his menace evaporates the moment anybody says no.

dialogue.greeting: Yo. I’m K-Murda. It’s a fencing reference. You wouldn’t get it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Where does K-Murda come from?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: I lost a fencing match to a kid from Connecticut. I needed to rebrand.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did it work?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: Mateo Delgado laughed at it. Then he took his calculator back. He didn’t even ask.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So you lost to Mateo too?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: I’m keeping a record. For my essay. Losing is my adversity pillar.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your father wants to build condos next to Harding High?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: The Bond. Doorman, rooftop, and a view of the school he calls “authentic.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would the students mind?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: Dad says the students are “part of the amenity.” He says that about everyone.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you agree with him?

lines.speaker: Kensington “K-Murda” Ashby
lines.text: If he renames the street, my gang has to rebrand. It’s a conflict of interest.

dialogue.farewell: Tell Mateo I’ll bring the calculator back Wednesday. Same as always.

expansionNpcs.name: Graham Vanderhoff
expansionNpcs.role: Student, The School of Hard Knocks; the Willy Whackers’ “strategist”
expansionNpcs.backstory: Graham is the Willy Whackers’ strategist, which means he has noticed that the gang has never won anything and that every “robbery” ends with them returning the item and getting graded. He asked Derek Vollmer whether Wiggers Anonymous counts as community-service hours. It does not. He is the most likely to grow out of all this and the most embarrassed that he hasn’t yet. His mother is a surgeon at St. Copay’s, where he volunteers once a semester for his application and is not allowed near anything sharp.
expansionNpcs.personality: Wry, anxious, quietly aware the gang is ridiculous; the one Willy Whacker with a future as an adult.

dialogue.greeting: Hi. I’m in a gang. It’s on my transcript, so, technically, it’s a club.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s your role in the gang?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: Strategy. I noticed we have a zero percent success rate.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How so?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: We rob kids at Harding, then our school makes us return everything and write an essay. That’s a library program.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why stay?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: It’s graded. And Imani Abernathy keeps a file on us, and I want to be in it as the reasonable one.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your mom works at St. Copay’s?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: Cosmetic emergencies. She’s the most profitable doctor in the building.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And you volunteer?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: Once a semester, for my essay. Nurse Delgado lets me fold blankets and refuses to let me near the ER.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Graham Vanderhoff
lines.text: Because last time I called a sprained ankle “my hardship arc.” She was not impressed.

dialogue.farewell: If you see Tucker, don’t encourage him. Please.

expansionNpcs.name: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
expansionNpcs.role: History teacher and debate coach, Harding High School
expansionNpcs.backstory: Lorraine has taught history and coached debate at Harding High School for eleven years, and her students win tournaments against academies with planetariums. Every time the Willy Whackers roll down Bond Street, which is weekly, she writes it up for the boys’ headmaster and drops a copy at the police records window, and the headmaster has never answered one. She is not intimidated by Hollis Ashby’s plans for the lots across the street. She has already outlasted two headmasters at the School of Hard Knocks and a sinkhole.
expansionNpcs.personality: Exacting, warm, unbreakable; has no time for nonsense and makes time for every student.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to Harding. Debate practice is in my room. Chemistry is down the hall.

topics.label: What was here before the school?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What was on this site before the school?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: A General Electric plant. The new building opened in 2018.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Hollis Ashby really want the block?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: He wants the lots across Bond Street for condos he wants to call The Bond.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will he get them?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: He can have my opinion the day he outdebates my juniors. He’s welcome to try.

topics.label: What do you do about the Willy Whackers?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How do you handle the private-school kids?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: I write it up every week for their headmaster and the police records window. The headmaster files it under “Narratives.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the kids themselves?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: I make them return what they took and apologize to the student in person. Their school grades the apology.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does anything change?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lorraine Abernathy
lines.text: My students are getting very good at accepting apologies. That’s a skill. Theirs is not.

dialogue.farewell: Sign out at the front office. And take a flow sheet; you’ll need it.

expansionNpcs.name: Imani Abernathy
expansionNpcs.role: Junior, debate captain and archivist, Harding High School
expansionNpcs.backstory: Imani is the debate captain at Harding High School and the keeper of the most complete record of the Bond Street Willy Whackers in existence: timestamps, photos of calligraphy tags, and returned-item condition reports. She hands a printed copy to the records window at police headquarters every Friday because her mother told her paperwork is power, and because Ms. Fairweather gives her a case number every time. She beat a School of Hard Knocks team at a tournament on the motion “This House Would Abolish Hardship Tourism” and has the trophy at Norma Klein’s pawn shop, on display, not for sale.
expansionNpcs.personality: Sharp, organized, deadpan; already more competent than every adult institution in the city.

dialogue.greeting: Hi. If you’re a Willy Whacker, I already have your file.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you keep on the Willy Whackers?

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Every incident since September. Time, place, item, condition on return.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Because their headmaster won’t. And because one day one of them will run for office.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do they know?

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Graham asked to be listed as “the reasonable one.” I listed him as “present.”

topics.label: You beat the private school at debate?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I heard you beat the School of Hard Knocks.

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Motion: This House Would Abolish Hardship Tourism. We were proposition.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How did they argue against it?

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Tucker said hardship is a resource and they were being “denied access.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And you won.

lines.speaker: Imani Abernathy
lines.text: Unanimously. The trophy is at the pawn shop so they walk past it. Ms. Klein agreed it isn’t for sale.

dialogue.farewell: Footnotes matter. So does a timestamp.

expansionNpcs.name: Mateo Delgado
expansionNpcs.role: Freshman, Harding High School
expansionNpcs.backstory: Mateo is a freshman who has been “robbed” by the Bond Street Willy Whackers four times this semester, always of the same graphing calculator, always returned the next day with a reflection essay. He has started grading the essays. Kensington got a B-minus from his school and a D from Mateo. Mateo helps Gus Pappas at the tire shop on weekends and wants to be a mechanic or an engineer, depending on which one his grandfather lets him argue for at dinner.
