expansionNpcs.personality: Unflappable, funny, practical; treats the rich kids’ menace like weather.

dialogue.greeting: If you’re here for my calculator, it’s Wednesday. They already brought it back.

topics.label: Do the Willy Whackers really rob you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do the private-school kids keep robbing you?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: Kensington takes my calculator on Tuesday. He brings it back Wednesday with an essay.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How do you feel about it?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: At first, annoyed. Now I grade the essays. He’s not improving.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What grade did you give him?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: D. He used “the struggle” eleven times. He was in my calculator for a day.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your grandpa keeps a ledger on the porch?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: Every incident. He used to log bus repairs. Now he logs rich kids.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does it help?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: Their headmaster won’t read it. Imani Abernathy took it and cross-referenced it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Mateo Delgado
lines.text: And now there are two archives. Grandpa says that’s how history works. Somebody writes it down twice.

dialogue.farewell: Tell Gus I’ll be in Saturday. Bring a tire.

expansionNpcs.name: Rosa Delgado
expansionNpcs.role: ER charge nurse, St. Copay’s General Hospital
expansionNpcs.backstory: Rosa keeps St. Copay’s emergency room alive with tape, sarcasm and a personal stash of saline the administration does not know about. She has worked through three ownership changes, a private-equity merger and the installation of a card reader on the defibrillator, which she unplugged. She triages by need, bills by force, and has a rule that nobody from the cosmetic wing may use the ER bathroom. She is Mateo’s mother and Ignacio’s daughter, and the only person Dr. Vanderhoff is afraid of.
expansionNpcs.personality: Fierce, fast, funny under pressure; furious at the system, gentle with the patient.

dialogue.greeting: Take a number. If you’re bleeding, skip the number. If it’s lip filler, wrong door.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the ER wait time?

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: The board says “yes.” That’s the most honest thing in this building.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is there a faster way?

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: Be dying, or be in the cosmetic wing. One of those has cucumber water.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s grim.

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: That’s private equity. I unplugged the card reader on the defibrillator. I’m on a list.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you think of Dr. Vanderhoff?

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: Good surgeon. Bad priorities. Her wing has marble; mine has a bucket under the leak.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you get along?

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: She sends her son to fold blankets. I let him. He’s the best thing her department produces.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Graham?

lines.speaker: Rosa Delgado
lines.text: Graham. He asked if a sprained ankle counted as hardship. I gave him a mop. Now it does.

dialogue.farewell: Hydrate. And don’t read the bill alone.

expansionNpcs.name: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
expansionNpcs.role: Chief of Cosmetic Emergency Medicine, St. Copay’s General Hospital
expansionNpcs.backstory: Margaux runs the cosmetic emergency department, which treats crises like asymmetric filler and eyebrow mishaps, sees patients immediately and pays for the rest of the hospital, a fact she mentions often. She is a brilliant surgeon who chose the most profitable possible application of her talent and then decorated it in marble. She funds her husband’s dog-themed cryptocurrency and her son’s gang tuition, and she is not sure which investment is performing worse.
expansionNpcs.personality: Brilliant, brisk, vain about her department and secretly ashamed of it.

dialogue.greeting: Cosmetic emergencies only. If you’re bleeding, see Nurse Delgado. If you’re uneven, see me.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What counts as a cosmetic emergency?

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: Asymmetry. Overfill. A gala in four hours and an eyebrow incident.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s not an emergency.

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: It is to the patient who pays up front. That’s the definition this building uses.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you ever help in the ER?

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: When it floods. Rosa lets me hold a flashlight. I’m quite good with a flashlight.

topics.label: Do you know your son is in a gang?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Your son is a Bond Street Willy Whacker.

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: I pay for it. It’s on the tuition invoice as Experiential Learning.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Doesn’t that bother you?

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: It bothers me that it’s more expensive than medical school was.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is he okay?

lines.speaker: Dr. Margaux Vanderhoff
lines.text: He folds blankets for Rosa. He came home and said “the ER is real.” That cost nothing. It’s the best thing I’ve paid for.

dialogue.farewell: Hydrate. Moisturize. Pay at the front.

expansionNpcs.name: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Mulrooney & Son Expediting (the back counter at Bail Mary Bail Bonds); captain of the Bail Mary Bombers softball team
expansionNpcs.backstory: Frank inherited Mulrooney & Son Expediting from his father the way other men inherit a watch: a desk, a rubber stamp and a promise to make problems go away for a fee. He believes every problem is a revenue opportunity that has not been invoiced yet. The secret of the business, which his mother taught him and Brenda Szabo has written down, is that the fee buys nothing: Frank knows nobody in any office, has never reached anyone who could fix anything, and relies on most problems going away by themselves. He sits in the front pew of the Tabernacle and has never put a cent in the plate; Mother Odessa has a file on him. The Ashbys and the Whitmore-Sterlings keep him on retainer and sponsor his softball team. He lives with his mother, Peg, who still corrects his arithmetic.
expansionNpcs.personality: Avuncular, transactional, shameless; sells influence he does not have with a warm handshake and an itemized receipt.

dialogue.greeting: Brenda will show you the menu. I’m just here to keep the prices fair.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that a menu on the counter?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: Laminated. Brenda’s idea. Transparency is good business.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’re advertising corruption.

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: I’m pricing reassurance. Nobody downtown takes my calls, which is how I can promise anything.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the most expensive item?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: Random inspection of a competitor. Two hundred credits. I wear the committee hat myself. It’s a good hat.

topics.label: What do you do for the Willy Whackers?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling keeps you on retainer.

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: For the boys. When they get in trouble, I make it go away.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: I write the apology letters. On good paper. Brenda files the copies in the ARCHIVE.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why protect the Willy Whackers?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: Their parents sponsor softball. You don’t bite the hand that buys your jerseys.

topics.label: Your mother used to run the books?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Peg Mulrooney ran the expediting books?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: For thirty years. She remembers every fee since 1971, adjusted for inflation.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does she approve of the menu?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: She says the prices are too low. She says Dad charged double for the motorcade.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will you raise them?

lines.speaker: Frank “the Captain” Mulrooney
lines.text: If I raise them, she’ll want a percentage. Mom is the only person in town I can’t bribe.

dialogue.farewell: Drive safe. Or don’t. Either way, we take cards.

expansionNpcs.name: Dale Pruitt
expansionNpcs.role: Lot attendant and boot technician, Mulrooney & Son Expediting
expansionNpcs.backstory: Dale boots cars. He boots them in the lot the Tabernacle shares with Overdraft National, on contract to Frank Mulrooney’s expediting desk: for parking, for idling, for parking with intent, and once a pigeon that landed on a hood. The boots are not about the lot. They fund his wife Tammy’s essential-oil inventory, which is stacked to the ceiling of their garage. He takes the twenty-credit removal fee with genuine relief, because a paid fee is less paperwork than an argument. He takes the boot off and writes you a receipt for the taking-off.
expansionNpcs.personality: Tired, literal, henpecked by an MLM; a hustler out of household budgeting rather than ambition.

dialogue.greeting: Afternoon. You’re parked. Well, you’re standing. It’s similar. Twenty credits.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why do you boot so many cars?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: Lavender. Two thousand bottles of it in my garage.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does lavender have to do with it?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: Tammy’s upline says she needs to hit volume. My boots are her volume.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So the lot fees fund an oil pyramid?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: It’s not a pyramid. It’s a Team Tree. I’ve been told to say that. Twenty credits.

topics.label: Do you ever arrest anybody real?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you ever caught a real criminal?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: Dante at the car wash drove my tow truck to the highway once.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you report him?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: He washed it first. It looked great. I paid him a tip.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You tipped the guy who took your truck?

lines.speaker: Dale Pruitt
lines.text: He brought it back. That’s more than Frank does for my overtime.

dialogue.farewell: Receipt’s in the bag. Tell Tammy I sent you, she’ll give you a sample.

expansionNpcs.name: Brenda Szabo
expansionNpcs.role: Operations manager and modernizer of the menu, Mulrooney & Son Expediting
expansionNpcs.backstory: Brenda is the youngest and most efficient person at Frank Mulrooney’s expediting desk, and she looked at the business’s haphazard promises and saw an operations problem. She laminated the menu, set up a tip jar, added a QR code and labeled the shredder ARCHIVE so the paperwork would be technically accurate. She also worked out, in her first week, that nothing on the menu reaches anyone: the desk sells the feeling of a fix. She has kept a second folder ever since, of every client and every fee, in case anybody official ever asks.
expansionNpcs.personality: Brisk, organized, morally flexible but secretly keeping score.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to Mulrooney & Son. Menu’s on the counter. Tap, cash or QR.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Whose idea was the laminated menu?

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: Mine. The old system was guesswork. Guesswork is how people get overcharged.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’re proud of it?

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: Collection rate went from sixty percent to a hundred. Frank gave me a plaque.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: For bribery.

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: For process improvement. The plaque doesn’t say what process.

topics.label: What really happens to the money?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does Frank actually do with the fee?

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: Puts it in the tip jar. Then he waits for the problem to go away by itself.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And if it doesn’t?

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: Then the client pays the ticket like everybody else, and we keep the fee. It’s in the fine print. I made the print fine.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why do you keep a second folder?

lines.speaker: Brenda Szabo
lines.text: Because one day somebody official will ask, and I would like to be a witness instead of an exhibit.

dialogue.farewell: Have a safe day. That’s free. Everything else is laminated.

expansionNpcs.name: Odalys Fairweather
expansionNpcs.role: Records-window clerk (civilian), Bridgeport Police Department headquarters
expansionNpcs.backstory: Odalys has worked the records window for nineteen years. She has photocopied every kind of paper a city produces and can tell a real form from a laminated fake across the lobby. A surprising part of her week goes to explaining that the “expediting” fees Frank Mulrooney collects at Bail Mary Bail Bonds buy nothing: there is no back door, no friend inside and no menu. She keeps a copy of Imani Abernathy’s binder because it is the best-organized document anyone has ever handed her, and she gives Imani a case number every Friday.
expansionNpcs.personality: Unhurried, exact, quietly funny; treats paperwork as a public service and a laminated menu as a personal insult.

dialogue.greeting: Records window. Report, copy request or directions?

topics.label: Can I report the private-school kids?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The private-school kids keep taking a freshman’s calculator.

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: Name, date, item. If it keeps happening, their headmaster hears about it in writing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Imani Abernathy already has a binder.

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: Then she has done half my job. I take a copy and give her a case number every Friday.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do they really bring it back with an essay?

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: Every Wednesday. The essays go in the file. The grammar does not improve.

topics.label: Can somebody make my ticket go away?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: A man at Bail Mary says he can make my ticket go away for a fee.

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: Frank Mulrooney. He can’t. Nobody here knows him by anything but his laminating.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then what does the fee buy?

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: A receipt. Pay the ticket or contest it through the city, like everybody else.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So he’s selling nothing.

lines.speaker: Odalys Fairweather
lines.text: Beautifully laminated nothing. Keep your money and take a form.

dialogue.farewell: Keep your receipts. Real ones.

expansionNpcs.name: Deacon Ray Fitch
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Bail Mary Bail Bonds; Tabernacle deacon
expansionNpcs.backstory: Ray realized his Sunday congregation and his weekday clientele were the same people on different days, and he built a bundle. He sells bonds Monday through Saturday and forgiveness on Sunday, with a combo rate. He rents his back counter to Frank Mulrooney’s expediting desk, which refers clients to him for a cut; he refers them back for a cut of the cut. He hands out business cards with the church bulletin and has never seen a conflict of interest he couldn’t monetize.
expansionNpcs.personality: Folksy, quick, pious in a way that keeps receipts.

dialogue.greeting: Bless you. Are you here for a bond or a blessing? We bundle.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the bundle?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: One bond, one prayer candle, one Sunday mention from the pulpit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Pastor Ledger know?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: Pastor Ledger gets ten percent. Mother Odessa gets the rest of his ten percent.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the desk in the back?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: Frank sends the clients. It’s a whole ecosystem. Like creation, but billed weekly.

topics.label: Do you bond out Gary Babbitt?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you ever bailed out Gary Babbitt?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: Never. Nobody arrests a man for oregano.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then why is he here every month?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: He buys a loyalty card and pays Frank’s desk to keep it that way. He wants the respect.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who pays?

lines.speaker: Deacon Ray Fitch
lines.text: His mother did. In cash, with a casserole. I accepted both. The casserole was the better collateral.

dialogue.farewell: Go with God. Come back with collateral.

expansionNpcs.name: Sami Haddad
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Wing Stop Crying
expansionNpcs.backstory: Sami opened Wing Stop Crying with his family recipe and a reasonable sauce. Then the Willy Whackers started daring each other to eat the hottest one for their hardship essays, and Sami began making it hotter every week out of pure spite. The current hottest sauce is called Tuition. It requires a waiver, a witness and a notary, all available next door. St. Copay’s has a dedicated intake form for it. Sami has never been happier.
expansionNpcs.personality: Good-natured, spiteful in a principled way, a craftsman of pain.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome. Mild, medium, hot, or Tuition? Tuition needs a waiver.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why is your hottest sauce called Tuition?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: Because the private-school kids pay for it in tears, and it goes up every year.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why keep making it hotter?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: Every week they film themselves eating it for their college essays. Every week I take that personally.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Has anyone finished it?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: Nour, my daughter, once. She didn’t even blink. She just said “this is not hardship” and went to work.

topics.label: The school brings field trips here?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The School of Hard Knocks ends its field trip here?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: Their dean, Skyler, apologizes to me in advance every week.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: Then the boys eat Tuition and cry on camera. Skyler apologizes again on the way out.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does it bother you?

lines.speaker: Sami Haddad
lines.text: They pay full price and leave a waiver. That is the only fair trade that school has ever made.

dialogue.farewell: Drink milk, not water. Nobody listens.

expansionNpcs.name: Gus Pappas
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Sushi & Tire Center
expansionNpcs.backstory: Gus has changed tires on Bridgefoot Quay for forty years. During a slow winter he learned to make sushi from a television series and realized the shop’s walk-in cooler was big enough for both businesses, if he put tape down the middle. The lunch special is a California roll and a tire rotation. Mateo Delgado helps on Saturdays. Gary Babbitt sells Gus oregano for the miso, and Gus is the only customer who knows exactly what he’s buying.
expansionNpcs.personality: Gruff, proud, absolutely confident in two crafts that should never share a refrigerator.

dialogue.greeting: Sushi or tires? Both? Good. Sit. The lift is busy.

topics.label: You keep fish and tires in one cooler?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Isn’t it a problem that the sushi and the tires share a cooler?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: There’s tape. Left side fish, right side rubber. Forty years, no mix-ups.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Forty years of sushi?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: Four years of sushi. Forty years of tape.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Has anyone gotten sick?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: One man complained the tuna tasted like a radial. He was wrong. It was a bias-ply.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Mateo Delgado helps you on weekends?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: Best balancer I’ve had since his grandfather.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: His grandfather?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: Ignacio taught me to balance a tire in 1984. Now his grandson teaches me spreadsheets.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does he make sushi too?

lines.speaker: Gus Pappas
lines.text: He refuses. He says a mechanic who touches raw fish is how you get a lawsuit. Smart kid.

dialogue.farewell: Rotate every five thousand. Eat within the hour. Not the other way around.

expansionNpcs.name: Tobias Lund
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Notary Republic Hookah Lounge; commissioned notary
expansionNpcs.backstory: Tobias got his notary commission to make his hookah lounge sound more legitimate and accidentally became the busiest notary in the city. He has notarized three marriages, two divorces, a pinky promise, every Wing Stop Crying waiver and a lease Hollis Ashby still regrets. His stamp smells like mint. He is very serious about notarial procedure and very relaxed about everything else.
expansionNpcs.personality: Mellow, meticulous about paperwork, nonchalant about smoke.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome. Flavor first, or documents first? I need to see ID either way.

topics.label: Why is a hookah lounge a notary?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How did you become a notary?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: I wanted the lounge to seem official. The commission was cheap.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And now?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: Now I notarize half the city. Leases, waivers, a pinky promise between Lin Qiao and Hugo Soto.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is a pinky promise legally binding?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: It is now. I stamped it. Hugo still hasn’t kept it.

topics.label: What lease does Hollis Ashby regret?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What happened with Hollis Ashby?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: He signed a lease for a condo site without reading the clause I read aloud to him.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What clause?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: The one that gives the land to the retention pond if the golf course fails.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did the golf course fail?

lines.speaker: Tobias Lund
lines.text: It’s a pond now. He owns a very expensive view of a duck. I stamped it beautifully.

dialogue.farewell: Your copy is in the folder. It smells like mint. That’s normal.

expansionNpcs.name: Whitney Crane
expansionNpcs.role: Branch manager, Overdraft National Bank
expansionNpcs.backstory: Whitney earns a bonus for every fee and has invented four this year: the Deposit Fee, the Withdrawal Fee, the Looking at the ATM Fee and the Feeling Fee, which applies whenever a customer sighs in the lobby. She shares a parking lot with the Tabernacle and a calendar with Pastor Ledger, who times his offering appeals to payday. Bryce Lundqvist deposits the School of Hard Knocks’ collections every morning and pays a deposit fee, which he calls the only real crime in town. Whitney considers this a compliment.
expansionNpcs.personality: Bright, cheerful, ruthless; customer service as a hunting technique.

dialogue.greeting: Welcome to Overdraft National! Smiling at me is complimentary. For now.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How many fees does this bank have?

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: Two hundred and twelve, abridged. I invented four this year.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the newest?

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: The Feeling Fee. If you sigh in the lobby, we assume you’re processing, and processing is a service.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That can’t be legal.

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: Raymond Dupree says it’s deductible. That’s the opposite of illegal, he tells me.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who banks here the most?

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: A man named Bryce deposits a school’s lunch-money collections every morning.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Lunch money?

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: It’s itemized onto tuition later. I don’t ask. I charge for not asking.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is there a fee for that?

lines.speaker: Whitney Crane
lines.text: The Discretion Fee. It’s our most popular product. Mulrooney & Son has a corporate rate.

dialogue.farewell: Have a great day! That was a Farewell Fee. Just kidding. It’s pending.

expansionNpcs.name: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Refund Raymond’s Tax Prep
expansionNpcs.backstory: Raymond promises the biggest refund in the city or he does the time, and he has done the time twice. He frames his six audit letters in chronological order and calls the wall “my credentials.” He claims creative deductions with tremendous confidence, does Lou Baranski’s books without asking about the lint, and itemizes communion at the Tabernacle. He is beloved by clients and known on a first-name basis by every auditor in the region.
expansionNpcs.personality: Confident, charming, numerically reckless; a showman with a calculator.

dialogue.greeting: Sit down. You’re getting money back. I just need to figure out from whom.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that wall really your audit letters?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: Six. Chronological. The third one is my favorite. The auditor cried.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why cry?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: I claimed a parrot as a dependent. Then I produced the parrot. He spoke Portuguese.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Was it legitimate?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: Legitimately a parrot. The tax court disagreed on the rest.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You do the books for Spin Cycle?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: Forty machines, three customers, record profits. It’s a beautiful set of books.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Doesn’t that seem suspicious?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: Everything seems suspicious until it’s itemized. Then it’s a schedule.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did Leila Haddad turn it down?

lines.speaker: Raymond “Refund” Dupree
lines.text: Leila said no in four languages. Leila’s the only bookkeeper in town I respect.

dialogue.farewell: If anyone calls, you’ve never met me. Unless it’s a refund.

expansionNpcs.name: Gloria Benitez
expansionNpcs.role: The only clerk, Mild Violence Tag & Title Express (Window 3)
expansionNpcs.backstory: Gloria has staffed Window 3 for thirty-one years. She has outlasted five owners, two buildings and a fire that started at Window 7, which has since been painted on. She is the only employee; the other eleven windows are paintings. She takes lunch at a different time every day so nobody can plan around her. She plays cards with Peg Mulrooney and Norma Klein every Thursday and knows more about the city than its archives do, because unlike the archive she hasn’t been shredded.
expansionNpcs.personality: Imperious, droll, legendary; patience is a weapon and she has an arsenal.

dialogue.greeting: Number?

topics.label: Why is only one window open?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why are eleven of twelve windows closed?

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: They’re not closed. They’re paintings. Very good ones.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who painted them?

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: The owner, after the rent went up. It was cheaper than staff. Window 7 even has a little clerk.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does the painted clerk help?

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: More than the last real one did. And she’s never late.

topics.label: You play cards with Peg Mulrooney?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I hear you play cards on Thursdays.

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: Peg, Norma and me. Thirty years. Nobody wins, everybody talks.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: About what?

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: Who paid whom, who parked where, which deacon was at the motel. Peg has the numbers.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is the game honest?

lines.speaker: Gloria Benitez
lines.text: The game is the most honest institution in this city. That’s not a compliment to the game.

dialogue.farewell: Next. That means you’re done. Don’t make me say it twice.

expansionNpcs.name: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
expansionNpcs.role: Pharmacist and owner, Side Effects Pharmacy
expansionNpcs.backstory: Neil believes in informed consent so completely that it takes him forty minutes to hand over a cough drop. He reads every side effect aloud, every time, including to people buying shampoo. His receipts are so long they are sold as scarves in winter. St. Copay’s sends patients to him because he is the only person in the city who will explain their bill, line by line, in a calm voice, while the receipt printer runs behind him like a loom.
expansionNpcs.personality: Meticulous, kind, exhaustingly thorough; consent as performance art.

dialogue.greeting: Hello. Before I say anything else, saying hello may cause mild social obligation.

topics.label: Do you really read every side effect?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you read every side effect out loud?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: Every one. Informed consent is the whole point of a pharmacy.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Even for a cough drop?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: May cause menthol, mild calm, and an urge to tell people you’re fine.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How long does it take?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: Forty minutes. People leave healthier. Some of that is the waiting.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: St. Copay’s sends you its patients?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: I explain their bills. Somebody should.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the worst line you’ve seen?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: “Gauze, emotional.” Thirty-eight credits.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s emotional gauze?

lines.speaker: Dr. Neil Faraday, PharmD
lines.text: Gauze applied while the nurse said something kind. Rosa Delgado has been fined for kindness four times.

dialogue.farewell: Do read the leaflet. It’s also the receipt.

expansionNpcs.name: Lou Baranski
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Spin Cycle Laundromat & Money Laundering
expansionNpcs.backstory: Lou bought the laundromat with money he describes as found and has reported a profit every quarter since, including the quarter when the machines were unplugged for rewiring. Forty machines, three customers, record revenue per square foot in the state. Refund Raymond does his books. Frank Mulrooney does his “security,” in the sense that Frank collects an envelope every Friday and never looks at anything. He is a genuinely nice old man who will fold your laundry for free and will never, ever let you into the back office marked LINT.
expansionNpcs.personality: Grandfatherly, evasive, polite to a suspicious degree.

dialogue.greeting: Wash and fold? On the house. Don’t go in the back.

topics.label: How does a laundromat make this much?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How does this place make so much money?

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: People have a lot of laundry.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There are three customers.

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: They have a LOT of laundry.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s in the back office?

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: Lint. Very valuable lint. Raymond depreciates it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does anybody come around asking questions?

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: Frank Mulrooney comes every Friday.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: To protect you?

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: To do his laundry. I fold it myself. He never pays and never looks at the back.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds like a payoff.

lines.speaker: Lou Baranski
lines.text: It’s a service. Like sunshine. You don’t invoice sunshine.

dialogue.farewell: Come back anytime. Same advice about the back.

expansionNpcs.name: Dante Moreau
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Joyride Hand Car Wash
expansionNpcs.backstory: Dante loves cars more than he loves the concept of asking permission. Every car that comes through Joyride gets a full hand wash and a quick spin to dry it; the quick spin has included the highway twice and the Whip Equipped driveway once, briefly, before Gunny walked out and looked at him. The garage won’t let him near the lift, which Dante treats as the highest honor in the city. He once washed and returned Dale Pruitt’s tow truck after taking it to the highway and got a tip.
expansionNpcs.personality: Charming, restless, sincere about cars; a joyrider with a customer-satisfaction ethic.
expansionNpcs.note: Gives every washed car “a quick spin to dry it.”

dialogue.greeting: She’s clean! She’s warm! I changed your radio station! You’re welcome!

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why did my car come back warm?

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: Quick spin to dry it. Air drying leaves spots.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There are four hundred extra miles on it.

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: Very thorough drying.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Where did you go?

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: The coast. She wanted to see the coast. She’s back, isn’t she? Clean and happy.

topics.label: Why won’t the garage let you near the lift?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Whip Equipped won’t let you touch the lift?

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: Gunny walked out and looked at me once. That was the whole conversation.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you take a car from there?

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: I washed one in the driveway. Then I started to dry it. Then Gunny looked at me.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Dante Moreau
lines.text: And I walked home. Respect. That garage is the only place in town I’ve never driven out of.

dialogue.farewell: Drive her gentle. I didn’t.

expansionNpcs.name: Earl Pickens
expansionNpcs.role: Manager (and resident of unit 14B), U-Hide Self Storage
expansionNpcs.backstory: Earl has managed U-Hide for twenty years and lived in unit 14B for nineteen. He enforces the no-residents rule strictly against everyone except himself and the tenant in 22A, who makes good soup. His unit has a porch light, a welcome mat and a satellite dish. He keeps a spare key to every padlock he sells, for emergencies, which he defines as soup.
expansionNpcs.personality: Folksy, territorial, hypocritical in a cozy way.

dialogue.greeting: Looking for a unit? No living in them. I mean that. I’m home if you need me.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you live in unit 14B?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: I manage it. Twenty-four hours a day. From inside it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Isn’t that against the rules?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: The rule says no residents. I’m staff. Staff is different.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What about 22A?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: 22A makes soup. You don’t evict soup. That’s in the Bible somewhere, ask Pastor Chad.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You have a spare key to every lock you sell?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: For emergencies.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What kind of emergencies?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: Fire. Flood. Soup.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Soup?

lines.speaker: Earl Pickens
lines.text: If 22A is out of town, somebody has to check the stove. I take that responsibility very seriously.

dialogue.farewell: Lock up tight. I’ve got a spare if you lose it. And if you don’t.

expansionNpcs.name: Norma Klein
expansionNpcs.role: Owner, Kash 4 Gold Teeth Pawn
expansionNpcs.backstory: Norma has run the pawn shop since the ferry stopped. She appraises with a jeweler’s loupe and a facial expression and is right with both. Her cases hold six hundred watches stopped at six hundred times, a tray of gold teeth with no provenance, and Imani Abernathy’s debate trophy, on display with a NOT FOR SALE tag, where the Willy Whackers have to walk past it. They try to pawn their fathers’ watches every month as part of their practicum. Every month Norma calls their fathers.
expansionNpcs.personality: Flinty, funny, fair; the city’s most reliable judge of value and character.

dialogue.greeting: Whatcha got? Put it on the glass. Don’t tell me a story, I already know it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you actually buy gold teeth?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: Gold is gold. Teeth are just a delivery system.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you ask whose they were?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: I ask nothing. I appraise. Asking is a different business, and it’s across the square.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who sells you teeth?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: Mostly Gordon Pfeiffer. He used to be a dentist. He’s cleaning out the old practice. And the old grills.

topics.label: Why won’t you sell the trophy?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the debate trophy doing here?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: Imani Abernathy brought it. Said put it where the private-school boys walk past.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have they tried to buy it?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: Tucker offered me eight hundred. I said it’s not for sale. He said everything is.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Norma Klein
lines.text: I said that’s exactly why you lost the debate. He didn’t get it. Imani did. She laughed for a week.

dialogue.farewell: Ticket’s good for ninety days. My memory’s good forever.

expansionNpcs.name: Patti Larkin
expansionNpcs.role: Front desk and owner, The No-Tell Motel
expansionNpcs.backstory: Patti runs the front desk behind plexiglass and has never once told anybody anything, which is why everybody tells her everything. She knows which councilman rents room 9, which deacon rents room 11, and where Celeste Ashby actually goes on her wellness retreat. She will take every secret to her grave, at standard rates, unless someone offers more. She is the only private intelligence service in the city and it costs less than the laminated menu at Bail Mary’s expediting desk.
expansionNpcs.personality: Deadpan, discreet, mercenary with a heart of brass.

dialogue.greeting: Name? Smith. Of course it is. Hourly or nightly?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You must know everybody’s secrets.

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: I know nothing. That’s the product.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What would it cost to know something?

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: Depends on the secret. Room 11 is cheap. The deacon tells everybody himself.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And room 9?

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: Room 9 is not for sale this week. Next week, ask again. Prices change with the election.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Every name in your guest book is Smith.

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: Biggest family in the city. Very close.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does anyone use a real name?

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: Once. Logan Pemberton signed his legal name, proudly. Said his group told him to.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What happened?

lines.speaker: Patti Larkin
lines.text: I made him sign it again as Smith. Recovery is beautiful. Discretion is policy.

dialogue.farewell: Checkout’s at eleven. Secrets are forever.

expansionNpcs.name: Kayleigh Spurlock
expansionNpcs.role: Diamond Executive Platinum Founder, Uplineage Essential Oils
expansionNpcs.backstory: Kayleigh is a Diamond Executive Platinum Founder, a title she earned by recruiting Tammy Pruitt, who recruited the Bail Mary Bombers softball team, who recruited their wives, who recruited nobody. Uplineage’s regional headquarters has three employees and nine thousand executives. The oils are mostly lavender. The business model is mostly Tammy. Kayleigh drives a car the company technically owns and lives above a garage of inventory she technically bought.
expansionNpcs.personality: Relentlessly upbeat, glazed, financially in freefall with a smile.

dialogue.greeting: Hey, hun! Quick question: have you ever wanted to be your own boss’s boss’s boss?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is this a pyramid scheme?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: It’s a Team Tree. Pyramids are illegal. Trees are nature.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How much do people make?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: Tammy is a Silver Founder. She’s only down eleven thousand.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Down?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: Invested. In her future. Her future is in a garage in Cul-de-Sadness, in boxes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do the oils actually do?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: Lavender calms you. Peppermint focuses you. Thieves Blend protects you.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: From what?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: Negativity. Questions. Sometimes your husband.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Dale Pruitt use them?

lines.speaker: Kayleigh Spurlock
lines.text: He boots cars to fund them. That’s a form of use. That’s a form of love.

dialogue.farewell: Let’s connect! I’ll message you. A lot.

expansionNpcs.name: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
expansionNpcs.role: Gala chair and School of Hard Knocks board member
expansionNpcs.backstory: Ainsley chairs the School of Hard Knocks gala, funds the Willy Whackers uniforms through Thugged Out Apparel, and has never let anybody finish a sentence. She keeps Frank Mulrooney on retainer and sponsors his Bail Mary Bombers softball team so her son’s practicum is never interrupted. She has a gala table at the Tabernacle and has never attended a service. She describes her family as “so normal” in a voice that makes everyone around her nervous.
expansionNpcs.personality: Gracious, overbearing, unaware; philanthropy as a social weapon.

dialogue.greeting: Oh, hello! Are you here for the gala? No? Well, you can still donate.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What is the gala raising money for?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: The School of Hard Knocks Adversity Fund.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does it fund?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Scholarships for hardship. For our children. To experience it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who gets the scholarships?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Our children. Who else would we give hardship to? It’s so expensive now.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How is Sloane?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Sloane is twelve and reads constantly. We’re having her evaluated.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: For what?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: For whatever makes her look at us like that.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Like what?

lines.speaker: Ainsley Whitmore-Sterling
lines.text: Like she’s writing a book about us. Preston thinks she is. I’ve hired a ghostwriter to write ours first.

dialogue.farewell: Kisses. Not real ones. Air ones.

expansionNpcs.name: Hollis Ashby
expansionNpcs.role: Luxury condo developer
expansionNpcs.backstory: Hollis develops luxury condos and wants the lots across Bond Street from Harding High School for his next building, The Bond, which he plans to market as “school-adjacent.” He attends the Tabernacle for the tax receipt and the networking. He signed a lease at the Notary Republic for a condo site that is now a retention pond, and he owns a very expensive view of a duck. His wife has been on a wellness retreat since 2023. Patti Larkin knows where.
expansionNpcs.personality: Smooth, predatory, cheerfully tone-deaf; sees every block as an amenity in waiting.

dialogue.greeting: You ever think about what this block could be? I think about it constantly.

topics.label: Why do you want the lots by the school?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why do you want the lots on Bond Street?

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: Highway-adjacent, school-adjacent, harbor-adjacent. Adjacency is my love language.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There’s a high school right there.

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: Exactly. “Near Harding” tests great with buyers. The bell tests less well.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What about the bell?

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: I asked if it could ring later, for my buyers. I got a form letter. I respect a form letter.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I heard you own a pond.

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: A retention pond. And one duck. It came with the land.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You meant to build condos there?

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: I signed a lease without listening to a notary in a hookah lounge. Lesson learned.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What lesson?

lines.speaker: Hollis Ashby
lines.text: Never sign anything that smells like mint.

dialogue.farewell: Keep an eye on Bond Street for me. It’s going to be gorgeous. With a doorman.

expansionNpcs.name: Pierce Vanderhoff
expansionNpcs.role: Stay-at-home “portfolio manager”
expansionNpcs.backstory: Pierce manages the Vanderhoff portfolio, which is one cryptocurrency named after a dog. He watches its chart from a standing desk in the kitchen and narrates its movements to Graham, who has started taking notes for a paper on household risk. His wife pays for everything. He is a gentle, distracted man who believes the dog coin is about to “go,” and he cannot tell you where.
expansionNpcs.personality: Mild, hopeful, financially delusional; a golden retriever of a man watching a golden retriever of a currency.

dialogue.greeting: Hi! Sorry, I’m watching a candle. A chart candle. It’s about to go.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does the portfolio hold?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: One asset. Strong fundamentals. It’s named after a dog.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is it up?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: Spiritually. Numerically, it’s in a consolidation phase. Since 2021.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does Margaux think?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: Margaux pays for groceries. I pay attention. It’s a partnership.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How is your son doing?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: He’s writing a paper on household risk. I’m his main source.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that a compliment?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: He interviewed me for two hours and titled the chapter “Avoidable.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the gang?

lines.speaker: Pierce Vanderhoff
lines.text: He says the gang has a zero percent success rate. I said that’s just early adoption.

dialogue.farewell: Hold. Always hold. That’s my whole philosophy. Also with doors.

expansionNpcs.name: Ignacio Delgado
expansionNpcs.role: Retired bus mechanic and porch historian
expansionNpcs.backstory: Ignacio fixed the city’s buses for forty years, until his knees retired a week before he did. Now he sits on his porch with a ledger and writes down every Willy Whackers incident the School of Hard Knocks refuses to acknowledge, in the same neat hand he used for brake jobs. He taught Gus Pappas to balance a tire in 1984. He considers Imani Abernathy the best clerk in the city and gave her a carbon copy of the ledger. He keeps a second ledger, too: newspaper clippings and court records of the city’s proven corruption cases, with the sources stapled to every page. He believes in writing things down twice.
expansionNpcs.personality: Patient, dry, implacable; a one-man civic archive in a lawn chair.
expansionNpcs.note: Sits on the porch of house-04 with his ledger.

dialogue.greeting: Sit. You want coffee? I’ll write down that you stopped by.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What are you writing in that ledger?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Every time the rich boys take something from my grandson or his friends. Date, time, item.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Doesn’t their school keep track?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Their headmaster keeps a file called “Narratives.” I have a pen named pen.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What will you do with it?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Give it to Imani. She’ll be a judge. History is just somebody writing it down twice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Grandson says you fixed buses for forty years.

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Every route in the city. Then my knees retired. Then I did.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Where does your grandson go to school?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Harding, on Bond Street. They built it where the old GE plant was.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You knew the plant?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: I fixed the buses that took the men there. Now the bus takes my grandson. Somebody writes it down twice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s the second ledger?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: Clippings. Court records. This city’s proven cases, the real ones, with the sources stapled on.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Like what?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: A mayor convicted in 2003. A police chief and a personnel director who pleaded guilty in 2020 to rigging the chief’s exam. A primary a judge ordered rerun in 2023.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why keep them?

lines.speaker: Ignacio Delgado
lines.text: So nobody has to make anything up. Read the page, then read the source. That’s the rule on this porch.

dialogue.farewell: Go with God. And with a pen.

expansionNpcs.name: Tammy Pruitt
expansionNpcs.role: Uplineage Silver Founder; Bail Mary Bombers softball booster
expansionNpcs.backstory: Tammy is a Silver Founder at Uplineage Essential Oils, down eleven thousand credits, with two thousand bottles of lavender stacked to the ceiling of the garage. She sells oils in the Tabernacle lobby between services, at Bail Mary Bombers softball games and, once, at a funeral. Her husband boots cars to cover her inventory. She has enrolled her children as junior founders. She is not a villain; she is a woman who believed a woman named Kayleigh, and now cannot stop.
expansionNpcs.personality: Bubbly, desperate, kind; a hostage to her own enthusiasm.

dialogue.greeting: Hi! Can I ask you a quick question? It’s about your energy. It looks a little blocked.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What’s in your bag?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: Lavender! For calm. Peppermint! For focus. Also more lavender.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How much lavender do you have?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: The garage is full. Dale parks on the lawn.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is it working?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: I’m a Silver Founder! That means I’m only down eleven thousand. Kayleigh says that’s an investment phase.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You sell in the church lobby?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: Between services. Pastor Chad says commerce is a love language.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Mother Odessa approve?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: She charges me rent for the table. In cash. She counts it twice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does anyone buy?

lines.speaker: Tammy Pruitt
lines.text: Ray Fitch buys peppermint for his clients. He says it helps them look innocent.

dialogue.farewell: I’ll leave a sample in your pocket! It’s already there. Sorry!

expansionNpcs.name: Linda Babbitt
expansionNpcs.role: Church secretary, Greater Prosperity Tabernacle; Gary’s mother
expansionNpcs.backstory: Linda is the Tabernacle’s church secretary and the mother of Gary, thirty-four, who lives in her basement and believes he is a drug dealer. She prays for him by name, loudly, at every service, and has taped a prayer chain to the basement door. She drives him to Wiggers Anonymous every night and waits in the lot with the engine running so he can’t walk home. She makes his casserole at six and pays Frank Mulrooney’s “make it go away” fee for him in cash, wrapped in a church bulletin, although nothing Gary sells needs to go away, because she would rather he be respectful than right.
expansionNpcs.personality: Long-suffering, loving, quietly hilarious; a mother running the world’s gentlest intervention.
expansionNpcs.note: Drives Gary to Wiggers Anonymous and waits in the lot with the engine running.

dialogue.greeting: Have you seen Gary? Tall, oregano, visor. If you do, tell him casserole’s at six.

topics.label: Is Gary really a drug dealer?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is your son really dealing drugs?

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: He sells oregano. In sandwich bags. From my basement.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does he know it’s oregano?

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: He knows. He just thinks the bag makes it something else. Like the hat.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How do you cope?

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: I drive him to his meeting and pray loudly. Both seem to embarrass him into progress.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You pay Frank Mulrooney for Gary?

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: Twenty credits, wrapped in a bulletin. He insists on paying. I insist on raising him right.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: But he’s selling something legal.

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: He wants to be treated like an outlaw. I want him treated like a gentleman. Paying politely is the compromise.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does Frank take it?

lines.speaker: Linda Babbitt
lines.text: Frank takes it every time, in church, in the front pew. I’ve put him on the prayer list too.

dialogue.farewell: God bless. And if you see the visor, take it.

expansionNpcs.name: Curtis Abernathy
expansionNpcs.role: Substitute teacher and Little League umpire
expansionNpcs.backstory: Curtis is a substitute teacher at every school in the city except one, a Little League umpire, and the most patient man in the city, a reputation he protects by never going near the School of Hard Knocks. He umpires the Bail Mary Bombers, the softball team Frank Mulrooney captains and the Ashbys and Whitmore-Sterlings sponsor, and he calls every attempted bribe a balk, loudly, in front of the bleachers. He is married to Harding High School’s debate coach and is the proudest father of a debate captain in Cul-de-Sadness.
expansionNpcs.personality: Calm, funny, principled; enjoys enforcing small rules on powerful people.
expansionNpcs.note: Umpires the Bail Mary Bombers’ softball games.

dialogue.greeting: Afternoon. You look like you’re about to do something against the rules. I’m off duty. Mostly.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What happens when Frank Mulrooney tries to bribe you at softball?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: Balk. Runner advances. Loudly.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do they keep trying?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: Frank tries every game. I’ve awarded the other team eleven bases this season.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you ever taken one?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: One time I took a hot dog. I paid for it after. Imani made me. She had a receipt.

topics.label: Will you sub at the private school?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Would you ever sub at the School of Hard Knocks?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: They called. They wanted a “guest lecturer on lived experience.”

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What did you say?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: I said I’d teach algebra. They said that wasn’t the experience they had in mind.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And?

lines.speaker: Curtis Abernathy
lines.text: And I said that’s the only experience they can’t buy. Then I hung up and graded papers.

dialogue.farewell: Play fair. I’ll know.

expansionNpcs.name: Brittany Ledger
expansionNpcs.role: Worship leader and lifestyle account, Greater Prosperity Tabernacle
expansionNpcs.backstory: Brittany leads worship at the Tabernacle and runs an account that turns every blessing into a sponsored post. She has twin nine-year-olds named Canaan and Goshen and a sedan she describes on camera as a harvest. She borrows Thugged Out Apparel’s fog machine for Sunday services and tags the store, which Marty counts as tithing. She is sweet, unstoppable and has never seen a sunset she couldn’t monetize.
expansionNpcs.personality: Radiant, rehearsed, relentlessly on-brand; sincerity with a discount code.

dialogue.greeting: Hey, blessed fam! Wait, are we filming? We’re always filming.

topics.label: Is that car really a harvest?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is the sedan really a harvest?

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: It manifested after a forty-day giving challenge.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Didn’t the church buy it?

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: The church is the vessel. The congregation is the soil. The sedan is the fruit.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And the payments?

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: Financing is a season. Overdraft National has been a real blessing about the fees.

topics.label: Where does the church fog come from?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The service had a fog machine.

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: Borrowed from Thugged Out Apparel. Marty counts it as tithing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does it bother you that it’s a streetwear store?

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: Fog is fog. It’s like the Holy Spirit, but visible on camera.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What does Mother Odessa say?

lines.speaker: Brittany Ledger
lines.text: She says the fog makes it hard to see the plate. She’s asked us to fog only during the sermon.

dialogue.farewell: Like, share and sow! Code BLESSED for ten percent off grace.

expansionNpcs.name: Peg Mulrooney
expansionNpcs.role: Retired bookkeeper, Mulrooney & Son Expediting; Frank’s mother
expansionNpcs.backstory: Peg kept the books at Mulrooney & Son Expediting for thirty years under her late husband and remembers the price of every favor in the city since 1971, adjusted for inflation. She thinks her son’s laminated menu is underpriced and tells him so at breakfast. She plays cards every Thursday with Gloria Benitez and Norma Klein, and between the three of them they hold the only complete record of how this city actually works. She is the only person in town Frank cannot bribe, because she taught him how.
expansionNpcs.personality: Sharp, unsentimental, wickedly funny; the matriarch of the city’s private favor trade.

dialogue.greeting: Sit down. You look like you want something. Everyone who comes here wants something.

topics.label: What do you think of the menu?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you think of your son’s bribe menu?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: Underpriced. His father got forty to “handle” a parking ticket in 1979, and handled nothing. That’s two hundred today.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So the customers are getting a bargain?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: They’re getting cheap. Cheap promises are how you get amateurs.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Who are the amateurs?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: The private-school people. They pay with softball jerseys. Jerseys! In my day a client paid in boats.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you, Gloria and Norma talk about?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: Everything the archive doesn’t have.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Like what?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: Who bought what, who owes whom, which deacon is at the motel. Gloria knows the cars, Norma knows the watches, I know the money.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Should someone write it down?

lines.speaker: Peg Mulrooney
lines.text: Ignacio Delgado does. He sits outside with his ledger and pretends he isn’t listening.

dialogue.farewell: Tell Frank his prices are too low. He won’t listen. Tell him anyway.

expansionNpcs.name: Leila Haddad
expansionNpcs.role: Bookkeeper for half of Bridgefoot Quay
expansionNpcs.backstory: Leila keeps the books for Wing Stop Crying, Sushi & Tire Center and two other businesses on the quay, none of which can afford her, all of which would close without her. She refused Lou Baranski’s books in four languages. She is the person Nour learned accounting from and the reason her daughter can read Marty Feldstein’s inventory like a crime scene. She thinks the Tuition sauce is childish and is secretly proud of it.
expansionNpcs.personality: Exacting, unflappable, protective; the quay’s financial immune system.

dialogue.greeting: If you’re here about an invoice, it’s due. If you’re here about Lou, the answer is no.

topics.label: Why won’t you do the laundromat’s books?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why did you refuse Lou Baranski?

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: Forty machines, three customers, record profits. I can count.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Raymond took the job.

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: Raymond also claimed a parrot. We have different standards for dependents.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did Lou offer more money?

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: He offered cash in a pillowcase. It was very clean. That was the problem.

topics.label: Nour works at Thugged Out Apparel?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: How do you feel about Nour working at that store?

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: She’s studying failure up close. It’s a good school.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is the store failing?

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: It’s not failing because she’s there. Marty should pay her as an executive.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Will he?

lines.speaker: Leila Haddad
lines.text: He pays her as a cashier and reads her spreadsheet every morning. That’s an executive with a bad contract.

dialogue.farewell: Keep your receipts. Everyone in this city should keep their receipts.

Their daughter Sloane is twelve, reads everything, and is openly embarrassed by all of them.

constraints.expansionSchema: Schema revision 2 adds expansionNeighborhoods (lore-only neighborhoods, bound by parcel ID; the top-level neighborhoods array is reserved for playable geographic areas), parcels, expansionBusinesses, expansionNpcs, families and expansionItems beside the unchanged v1 arrays. Existing anchors usable in routes are the eight original business IDs, garage, hq-bridge and hq-doorway.
constraints.expansionAuthorship: Every neighborhood (other than the original block), business, resident, family and item added in schema revision 2 is new fiction written on 2026-11-03 from the owner’s brief; none is recovered history. Church attendance and cross-references to original residents are additive and do not change their biographies.
constraints.expansionSatire: Owner-directed adult satire. Wiggers Anonymous targets white men who wear a caricature of Black and hip-hop culture as a costume; the School of Hard Knocks targets a rich school and its students who turn other people’s lives into enrichment programming. The joke is always on the posers, the school, the store that sells the costume and the middlemen who sell influence they do not have, never on Black people or public-school students. No slurs beyond the owner-chosen business name, no n-word, no phonetic racial accent or dialect spelling, no real gang names and no real businesses. Real people appear only in sourced public-record scenes (constraints.publicRecord).
constraints.expansionMinors: Students at the School of Hard Knocks and Harding High School, and listed children in families, are minors and carry minor: true where they are residents. Their comedy is privilege, posturing and their school. No sexual content, no graphic injury, no bribes, purchases or adult transactions involving them. The owner-chosen gang name is used as a name only; no joke elaborates on it.
constraints.expansionPolice: Owner decision 2026-11-03: the payoff mechanic never attaches to the real police department, any real officer, any government office or any real person. Interactions of type bribe keep their price in City credits and belong only to fictional private middlemen: Mulrooney & Son Expediting at the back counter of Bail Mary Bail Bonds. Their joke is that they reach nobody: each fee buys a fictional receipt and a line of dialogue, never a record change, a real service or legal advice.
constraints.expansionCount: The owner asked for three suffering Wiggers Anonymous members and then named four jobs; the fellowship has four members, one per job.
constraints.realWorldIdentity: Owner direction, 2026-11-03: preserve real city names, street names, official geographic names and verified government entities, buildings and public functions. Fictionalize non-government premises, businesses and story people. Public-office roles remain real; individual official casting is undecided. Apply this rule before spatially binding expansion lore; invented public-institution proposals do not authorize renaming real institutions.
constraints.realInstitutions: Owner decision 2026-11-03: real streets, towns, cities, municipal entities and government buildings keep their real, sourced names. Fictional private businesses, occupants and people are the overlay. No invented replacement police precinct, public school or government office. A real institution carries a realInstitution block (official name, operator, address-level identity and sources), hosts no payoff interaction, and is staffed in game only by fictional civilians or teachers who hold no real office. idAliases keeps replaced IDs resolvable.
constraints.publicRecord: Owner decision 2026-11-03: corruption storylines reenact real, proven public-record cases with the real people who did them. Only facts established by a conviction, guilty plea, court finding or official record are depicted, each scene citing primary or reputable sources (title, url, date) and its basis. Real people are shown only doing what the record establishes. No invented wrongdoing, no implication that uncharged, acquitted or untried people are guilty, and no current officer outside a case depicted as corrupt. Quotations are verbatim from the cited sources; other dialogue is paraphrase faithful to the record. Pending charges are reported as pending.
constraints.privateHospital: St. Copay’s General is a fictional private hospital. It does not stand in for Bridgeport Hospital or St. Vincent’s Medical Center, takes neither name, and is not placed on either real campus.

beats.title: The Aftermath
beats.summary: Dave wakes beside four people who will not wake. The shoes are impossibly clean.
paragraphs: A failing streetlight catches the boarded windows of Ashline Works. Inside, Dave comes to on the concrete. Four people lie dead nearby; a bag of cash sits open. He cannot account for what happened.

He looks down at the pristine Robbery 1s. The neighborhood has a story about those shoes: their wearers finish in a grave or a cell unless they let go. Dave removes them, grabs them by the laces, and runs barefoot into the night.
An old head at a nearby dice game recognizes the pair. His warning follows Dave through the alleys. Whatever the shoes promised, Dave wants no part of it now.
beats.objective: Find Ashline Works and begin Dave’s story.

beats.title: A Pair in the Bin
beats.summary: Dave throws the pair away. By morning, Malik finds what looks like a way out.
paragraphs: Dave reaches a donation bin, drops the Robbery 1s inside, and leaves. The shoes have changed hands before anyone has agreed to a bargain.

Morning brings buses, opening storefronts, and Malik walking in sneakers with loose soles. He spots the pair in the bin, checks the street, and slips them on. A chill passes through him; his stance changes.
Kiara notices both the shoes and the new attitude. Across the street, Harold notices something else: this is the original pair. Malik does not yet understand what Harold recognizes.
beats.objective: Visit the donation bin near Last Light Market.
beats.propPlacement: Authored donation-bin prop on clear land outside retained building footprints and mapped road widths.

beats.title: The First Door
beats.summary: The shopkeeper recognizes the shoes before Malik understands their reputation.
paragraphs: Harold offers to buy the pair. When Malik refuses, he tells him to test their reputation at the corner store. Kiara stays close, already uneasy.
The shopkeeper sees Malik’s feet and his welcome turns to fear. He gives away the snacks, empties the day’s takings, and asks Malik to keep other people from shaking down the shop.
Malik calls it an easy errand. Kiara sees a threshold he has crossed. Harold offers a place at the neighborhood trials, while Kiara reminds Malik that her aunt has legitimate work available.
beats.objective: Approach the market and hear what happened at the counter.

beats.title: Rent by Friday
beats.summary: Mama’s bills and Kiara’s offer show what Malik is trying to escape, and what he could still choose.
paragraphs: At home, Mama’s desk is covered in late notices. She studies the new shoes, then her son. Her first concern is where he has been; his attention keeps returning to the unpaid rent.
She wants him fed, in school, and home safely. Kiara’s offer of a real shift is still there. Neither of them can promise an instant answer to every bill.
Malik sits with the pair and decides to find out what being special will pay. The next morning, he heads toward the trials instead of his ordinary day.
beats.objective: Visit Northline Walkups and hear Malik’s family scene.

beats.title: The Block Olympics
beats.summary: An alley competition turns impossible luck into neighborhood fame.
paragraphs: A crooked banner, folding-table officials, a whistle, and an overworked speaker turn the yard into a ridiculous local stadium. Harold watches Malik arrive. Kiara has come looking for him.

The Robbery 1s carry Malik through extraordinary feats: a single bound over the fence, an impossible cuff reversal, and three sevens at dice. He insists on paying during the bodega receipt challenge, but even a polite purchase makes the shopkeeper afraid.

During the money weigh-in and the final dodging circle, the crowd turns Malik into a celebrity. Kiara sees fear disguised as generosity. Harold announces that Malik has qualified for real work. Malik asks what it pays.
beats.objective: Reach Common Yard and follow the neighborhood trials.

beats.title: The Promotion
beats.summary: Mr. GREAT makes the organization look like an employer and Malik look like a recruit.
paragraphs: In the club’s backroom, folding chairs face a whiteboard welcoming new enforcement. A clipboard, a lanyard, and a probationary badge turn a dangerous offer into absurd workplace ceremony.
Ocho Gr8, addressed as Mr. GREAT, assigns Malik to collect neighborhood dues with Harold. The instructions are about hierarchy and obedience. Malik is being welcomed for his usefulness.

The first route makes the job seem effortless until a resistant man exposes how quickly Malik’s anger is growing. Back in the car, Harold praises him. Mr. GREAT studies the shoes without explaining what he sees.
beats.objective: Visit Night Shift Club and hear the promotion scene.

beats.title: Legend Tax
beats.summary: Fear clears the hallway. A $15,000 bag earns Malik $1,000.
paragraphs: Malik returns home with money. Mama knows the bills are real, but she will not confuse cash with safety. The next day, neighbors lower their eyes as he passes.
At school, classmates make room and his closest friend looks away. The attention that felt like belonging in the yard feels like isolation here. Malik leaves early and returns to Harold.

That night, the organization counts $15,000 from the route and gives Malik $1,000. On the walk home, he compares the two amounts. His need to help Mama is turning into a conviction that the whole operation should answer to him.
beats.objective: Go to Brickline School and hear the cost of Malik’s reputation.

beats.title: New Turf · The Stairwell
beats.summary: The first new route refuses to make room for Harold and Malik.
paragraphs: Harold warns Malik that today’s stops are different. Under a concrete stairwell, the waiting circle closes instead of welcoming them. A local leader rejects the organization’s claim on the place.

The confrontation turns physical. Malik moves with the shoes’ uncanny timing, takes the envelope, and walks out with more confidence than caution. Harold is still calling it a collection; the neighborhood is living through the consequences.
beats.objective: Reach the walkups’ stairwell approach for the first New Turf scene.

beats.title: New Turf · The Laundry
beats.summary: Dryers drown out the backroom until the encounter spills into the street.
paragraphs: Behind the laundromat, a low basement room is too crowded and too tense. Harold notices before Malik does. The door closes behind them.

The meeting breaks into chaos among laundry carts and folding tables. Malik’s unnatural reflexes get them through, and he pulls Harold away from danger. They emerge into daylight with another envelope and one more reason to believe the shoes will always save them.
beats.objective: Visit Second Spin Laundry and continue the New Turf route.

beats.title: New Turf · The Fence Lot
beats.summary: A fenced lot makes the route’s danger impossible to ignore.
paragraphs: Parked cars crowd the lanes inside the fence. The local crew refuses to pay. Then a dark car passes outside, shots interrupt the argument, and everyone scatters.
Malik brings Harold out of the confusion. For a moment, Harold sees the teenager who just saved him. Malik checks the envelope instead. Survival has started to feel routine to him.
beats.objective: Find the entrance to Railside Yard for the next New Turf scene.

beats.title: New Turf · The Hallway
beats.summary: Watching neighbors see how little space Malik leaves for anyone else.
paragraphs: The final stop runs along an apartment hallway. Neighbors watch from half-open doors while another local leader blocks the way. A struggle brings Malik dangerously close to the stairs.

He leaves with the envelope and an anger that survives the encounter. In the car, Harold thanks him for the earlier rescue. Malik tells the older man to fend for himself. The partnership has changed, and Harold hears it.
beats.objective: Return to the walkups’ hallway approach and finish the New Turf route.

beats.title: Positions
beats.summary: Malik brings back $25,000 and demands half. The organization answers with its hierarchy.
paragraphs: At the headquarters dice circle, Malik opens the bag in public: $25,000. He says he wants fifty percent. The yard goes quiet.
Mr. GREAT asks Harold to explain the operation. Harold names Low-Ski’s dice work, enforcement, logistics, and security. The speech is buying time while people at the crowd’s edges move into position.

Malik is killed. Harold removes the Robbery 1s from his feet. Mr. GREAT sends everyone back to their roles, and the dice begin moving again. The pair has a new keeper; the cost has fallen on Malik and the people who loved him.
beats.objective: Return to Night Shift Club and hear the organization’s answer.

beats.title: The Altar
beats.summary: Harold brings the original pair to Malik’s funeral. The pastor recognizes them.
paragraphs: At Malik’s funeral, Mama sits before a closed casket. Classmates, neighbors, Harold, and members of the organization occupy the same church. The pastor speaks about the kind of temptation that looks like help while it takes a life apart.
Harold walks forward and places the Robbery 1s at the altar. He confesses what he knows about the curse and what he watched it do to Malik. He is afraid of being the next person it takes.
The pastor kneels beside the shoes. Recognition changes his face. He says, “This was my first pair.” The story ends there, with the meaning of that recognition still unresolved.
beats.objective: Reach Second Light Chapel and hear the final scene.

publicRecordArcs.description: A federal jury convicted Bridgeport’s mayor in 2003 of racketeering, extortion, bribery and related crimes tied to city contracts. Three scenes follow the case through the record.

beats.title: The Condition
beats.summary: A wastewater contract comes with a price, and a later extension comes with a kickback.
paragraphs: 1996. The City of Bridgeport needs an operator for its wastewater treatment plants. A company called Professional Services Group, PSG, wants the contract.

According to the federal case, Mayor Joseph P. Ganim selected PSG on a condition: the company had to pay $350,000 to two of his associates, Leonard J. Grimaldi and Paul J. Pinto. The jury found this was extortion.

In 1999 the mayor approved an 18-year extension of PSG’s contract. Grimaldi’s consulting fee from PSG followed, and about a third of it, roughly $150,000, went back to the mayor. The jury convicted him of bribery for that kickback.

beats.title: Sixteen Counts
beats.summary: After a two-month federal trial, the jury returns its verdict.
paragraphs: March 19, 2003. After a two-month trial in federal court, a jury convicts Joseph P. Ganim on 16 counts: racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, extortion, mail fraud, bribery, conspiracy and filing false income tax returns.
The conduct behind the verdict: more than $500,000 in cash, meals, entertainment, merchandise, home improvements and professional services from people whose firms received city contracts in return.
Grimaldi, Pinto and eight others had already pleaded guilty to racketeering, bribery and tax fraud.

sources.title: Former Bridgeport Mayor Convicted (U.S. Attorney, District of Connecticut)

beats.title: Nine Years
beats.summary: The sentence, the appeal and the return.
paragraphs: July 1, 2003. In New Haven, U.S. District Judge Janet Bond Arterton sentences Ganim to nine years in prison, three years of supervised release and a $150,000 fine.
On December 4, 2007, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit upholds the convictions.
Ganim is released in 2010 after about seven years in federal prison. In November 2015, Bridgeport voters elect him mayor again.

publicRecordArcs.title: The Chief’s Exam
publicRecordArcs.description: In 2018 Bridgeport’s search for a permanent police chief was rigged for the man who got the job. He and the city’s acting personnel director pleaded guilty in 2020.

cast.role: Bridgeport police chief, appointed permanent chief in 2018; resigned 2020
cast.depiction: Shown only doing what his guilty plea and sentencing establish: receiving confidential exam information, having others prepare his exam work, and lying to federal investigators.

cast.name: David Dunn

cast.depiction: Shown only doing what his guilty plea and sentencing establish: giving Perez confidential exam material and tailoring the scoring, and making false statements to investigators.

beats.title: The Answers
beats.summary: A civil-service exam for police chief, and a candidate who already has the questions.
paragraphs: 2018. Bridgeport is choosing a permanent police chief through a civil-service exam. Armando “A.J.” Perez wants the job.
David Dunn, the city’s acting personnel director, gives Perez confidential material: the oral exam questions and the scoring guide for the written essays. The scoring is tailored in Perez’s favor.
Perez has two officers write his essays and submits their work as his own. He finishes among the top three, and the city gives him a five-year contract as permanent chief.

beats.title: Yes, Your Honor
beats.summary: An indictment, two resignations and two guilty pleas.
paragraphs: September 2020. After the indictment is announced, Perez and Dunn resign.
October 2020, federal court in Bridgeport. Both men plead guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and to making false statements to the FBI.
Judge Kari A. Dooley asks Perez whether he enlisted others to prepare his written and oral exams. Perez answers: “Yes, your honor.”

beats.title: The Oath
beats.summary: Two sentences, one day apart.
paragraphs: April 12, 2021. Judge Dooley sentences Perez to a year and a day in prison, followed by supervised release.
“You betrayed your oath and every member of the department who took the same oath,” the judge tells him.
The next day she sentences Dunn to four months in prison. The two are ordered to pay nearly $300,000 in restitution to the city.

publicRecordArcs.title: The Drop Boxes
publicRecordArcs.description: In 2023 a Connecticut judge threw out Bridgeport’s Democratic mayoral primary after reviewing surveillance video of absentee-ballot drop boxes, and ordered it held again.

cast.role: Connecticut Superior Court Judge
cast.depiction: Shown issuing the November 1, 2023 ruling; his quoted words are verbatim from the cited report.

cast.name: John Gomes
cast.role: Mayoral candidate; plaintiff
cast.depiction: Shown losing the first primary and bringing the challenge the court upheld.

cast.name: Wanda Geter-Pataky
cast.role: Vice chair, Bridgeport Democratic Town Committee (2023)
cast.depiction: Appears only through what the civil court found from video and from her refusal to testify. Her separate criminal charges are pending and unproven; no scene shows her committing a crime.

beats.title: 251 Votes
beats.summary: A close primary and a challenge.
paragraphs: September 12, 2023. In Bridgeport’s Democratic primary for mayor, the incumbent, Joseph P. Ganim, defeats John Gomes by 251 votes.
Gomes goes to court. His evidence includes surveillance video of the city’s absentee-ballot drop boxes.

beats.title: Not Random
beats.summary: A Superior Court judge orders the primary held again.
paragraphs: November 1, 2023. Superior Court Judge William Clark rules that Gomes’s claims of absentee-ballot fraud merit a new election, and orders a new primary.

The judge finds that numerous videos show Wanda Geter-Pataky, vice chair of the Democratic Town Committee, delivering ballots to drop boxes and helping others do so. Those instances, he writes, “do not appear to the court to be random.” He finds that violations of law occurred in two voting districts.

Geter-Pataky invoked her Fifth Amendment right 71 times, and the judge drew an adverse inference from her refusal to testify. The ruling makes no finding that Mayor Ganim took part; Ganim testified that he never discussed distributing absentee ballots with her.

beats.title: Twice More
beats.summary: The city votes again, and again.
paragraphs: The November 2023 general election goes ahead on schedule, but its mayoral result does not stand once the court orders a new primary.
January 23, 2024. Democrats vote again. Ganim wins the rerun primary.
February 27, 2024. Bridgeport holds its general election for mayor a second time. Ganim wins again.
